questions.concept_tag: Narrative Passage - sequence and detail
questions.question_text:
Passage: Rohan's first attempt to ride a bicycle ended in the mud. The lane was narrow, with a ditch running along one side, and the rain of the previous night had left it slippery. His father held the seat at the back and ran along the lane, promising never to let go. For a few seconds Rohan felt the thrill of balance; then he looked behind, saw that his father was standing far away with his hands in the air, and fell sideways into the ditch. Rohan was angry, not because he was hurt, but because he felt he had been tricked. His father laughed so loudly that a neighbour came out to see what had happened. 'You were riding by yourself,' he said. 'I let go ten metres back.' Rohan did not want to believe it. He wiped the mud from his knees and refused to try again that day. At night he lay awake, thinking about those few seconds. The next morning he went out alone, dragged the bicycle to the end of the lane and climbed onto it. He pushed off, wobbled, put down his foot and tried again. This time he did not look back. By the third attempt he could ride fifty steps without falling. When his father came out at noon, Rohan rode past him with his head high and did not say a word. His father, who knew when to stay silent, simply stepped aside and watched his son disappear around the corner with a smile that he made no effort to hide.

Why did Rohan fall into the ditch?

options.A: He looked back and realised that his father had let go.
options.B: His father pushed the bicycle too hard.
options.C: The bicycle was too big for him.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says Rohan felt the thrill of balance, then looked behind, saw his father standing far away with his hands in the air, and fell sideways. So he fell after looking back and realising his father had let go. Shortcut: for a sequence question, read the sentence just before the event for the cause. Trap (B): Reversal: the father had let go; he was not pushing. Trap (C): Out-of-scope: the size of the bicycle is not mentioned. Trap (D): Out-of-scope: the neighbour came after the fall.

questions.concept_tag: Discursive Passage - writer's attitude
questions.question_text:
Passage: Many students believe that staying awake late at night to study is a sign of dedication. They talk with pride about the number of hours they worked before an examination and sometimes compete with their friends over who slept least. Some students also rely on large amounts of tea or coffee to stay awake, which only hides tiredness for a short time. Research on sleep, however, points in a different direction. During sleep, the brain sorts and stores the things that were learned during the day. A student who studies for a long time and then sleeps well often remembers more than one who studies for the same time but gets very little rest. Lack of sleep also makes it harder to pay attention, to solve problems and to stay calm. This does not mean that a student should sleep all day or avoid hard work. It means that rest is part of learning, just as practice is. Teachers can help by avoiding the habit of setting tests early in the morning after students have spent the whole night preparing. Parents can help by encouraging regular meal times and bedtimes, rather than praising children for studying through the night. The student who sleeps seven or eight hours is not lazy; he is being sensible. Respecting sleep is not a luxury to be enjoyed after the work is done. It is one of the tools that make the work effective. A little less pride in staying awake, and a little more attention to rest, would help many students to learn better and to feel better as well.

The writer's attitude towards students who study through the night is best described as
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The writer questions the pride in sleepless study, explains the benefits of rest and offers gentle advice to teachers and parents. The attitude is concerned but sympathetic. Shortcut: look at the verbs and advice: the writer suggests and explains instead of blaming. Trap (A): Reversal: the writer does not admire the habit; the passage questions it. Trap (B): the writer blames a mistaken belief and gives advice calmly; there is no anger or scorn towards the students. Trap (D): Reversal: the writer clearly cares about the effects on learning.

questions.concept_tag: Reflective Passage - main idea
questions.question_text:
Passage: There was a time when the arrival of a letter was an event. The postman's bicycle bell could be heard in the lane, and children ran to the gate to see whether anything had come for them. A letter took days to travel, and so it carried the sender's thoughts as they had been on the day of writing. The handwriting showed the writer's mood; a hurried line, a smudge of ink or a pressed flower told something that words alone could not. People kept letters in boxes and read them again years later. A birthday card from a distant aunt, written in an unsteady hand, could be kept on the shelf for months. Today a message reaches us in a moment, and the speed is a gift. A mother can send a photograph to her son abroad, and a friend can reply to a question before the cup of tea has gone cold. But speed has a price. Messages are written quickly and are forgotten as quickly; very few of them are kept, and fewer still are read twice. We have gained the power to speak to each other at any time, but we may have lost the habit of saying something worth keeping. This does not mean that we should give up our phones and return to ink. It only suggests that, now and then, a person might sit down and write a few careful lines on paper, and by doing so, give a friend something that cannot be deleted by a single touch.

What is the central idea of the passage?

options.A: Letters are always better than modern messages.
options.B: Postmen should return to delivering letters on bicycles.
options.C: People today do not communicate at all.
options.D: Quick modern messages have benefits, but letters had a lasting value that we may miss.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The writer remembers the value of letters, accepts the gift of speed, and notes the loss of lasting messages. The final suggestion is to write a careful letter now and then. The central idea is a balanced one: modern messages have benefits, but letters had a lasting value. Shortcut: avoid options with 'always' or 'never' when the writer admits both sides. Trap (A): Extreme scope: the writer accepts that speed is a gift. Trap (B): Out-of-scope: the passage does not give any such suggestion. Trap (C): Reversal: the passage says that we can speak to each other at any time.

questions.concept_tag: Factual Passage - inference
questions.question_text:
Passage: Mangrove forests grow along coasts, in places where the land meets the sea and where the water is salty. Most trees would die in such conditions, but mangroves have found ways to live there. Some of them take in water through their roots and then push the salt out through their leaves, where it can sometimes be seen as small white crystals. Others have special roots that rise above the mud like pipes and let the tree breathe air even when the lower part is under water. These tangled roots do more than help the trees survive. They slow down the movement of waves and catch the mud and sand that the water carries, so the land at the edge of the sea slowly becomes firmer. During storms, a belt of mangroves can reduce the force of the waves before they reach the villages behind. The roots also shelter young fish, crabs and shrimps, which hide among them until they are large enough to survive in open water. For this reason, fishing communities near mangrove forests often have a steadier catch than those without them.  Local people have long used the fallen branches as firewood and the leaves as fodder, taking only what the forest can replace. Despite these benefits, mangroves have been cleared in many places to make room for farms, ponds and buildings. People who do this often discover, after some years, that the coast erodes faster and that the fish have grown fewer. The protection that was given freely by nature then has to be replaced by costly walls and repairs.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: Mangroves grow well in fresh water alone.
options.B: Clearing mangroves can eventually harm the coast and the people who live there.
options.C: Walls and repairs are cheaper than mangroves.
options.D: All fish live only among mangrove roots.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says that clearing mangroves leads to faster erosion, fewer fish and the need for costly walls. So it can be inferred that clearing mangroves can eventually harm the coast and its people. Shortcut: an inference follows from what the passage says about cause and effect near the end. Trap (A): Reversal: they grow where the water is salty. Trap (C): Reversal: the passage calls walls and repairs costly. Trap (D): Extreme scope: only young fish and other small creatures are said to shelter there.

questions.concept_tag: Discursive Passage - title
questions.question_text:
Passage: A festival is never only about the day on which it is held. Weeks before the event, the streets begin to change. Lamps and flags appear, shopkeepers repaint their doors, and in many homes the smell of sweets being prepared drifts through the windows. Families who live far apart make plans to travel so that they can be together. Neighbours who passed one another without a word during the year find themselves sharing a ladder to hang decorations. Even the youngest children take a part, carrying small lamps or helping to string flowers across the doors. Cooking, cleaning and decorating become shared tasks rather than burdens. In this way, a festival draws people out of their daily routines and into one another's company. Of course, each festival has its own meaning. Some mark the end of a harvest, some remember a story of courage, and others celebrate the changing of the seasons. But whatever its origin, a festival nearly always gives people a reason to gather, to give, and to forgive. Disputes are set aside, gifts are exchanged and the old are visited. Even those who are not religious often feel the pull of the occasion, because the real gift of a festival is a shared mood of gladness. It reminds communities that they are made of people who depend on one another. In an age when many of us spend hours alone with our devices, such days are more precious than ever. They teach us that happiness grows when it is shared, and that a street full of lamps is bright because many hands have lit them.

Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.A: The History of Lamps and Flags
options.C: Festivals: Occasions That Bring People Together

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage explains how festivals change a neighbourhood and bring people closer. The title that covers the whole idea is 'Festivals: Occasions That Bring People Together'. Shortcut: avoid titles based on a single detail such as sweets or lamps. Trap (A): Out-of-scope: the passage does not trace any history of lamps and flags. Trap (B): Reversal: the writer values festivals highly. Trap (D): Half-true: sweets are mentioned only as one detail of the preparation.

questions.concept_tag: Literary Passage - vocabulary in context
questions.question_text:
Passage: Silence is not the same as emptiness. On a winter evening in the hills, when the wind drops and the last bird has gone to its nest, the quiet that settles over the valley is full of small things. One can hear the faint creak of a branch, a distant dog, the soft fall of a pine needle on dry leaves. Even the stream, which seemed silent in daylight, can be heard murmuring. Travellers who have crossed mountain passes at night often say that the quiet seemed to have a weight of its own, a weight that was not unpleasant. The mind, which spends the day in constant noise, grows still and begins to notice what it had missed. People who live in cities often say that they cannot sleep in such a place, because the silence feels too loud. They have grown used to a steady hum of traffic and voices, and without it they feel uneasy. Yet those who stay for a few days often change their view. They discover that silence gives them back the habit of listening, not only to the world around them but also to their own thoughts. A thought that would have been drowned by noise in the city comes forward calmly and can be examined. This is perhaps why poets and thinkers have always sought quiet places. They did not wish to escape from people, but to find the space in which ideas could grow. In a world that rewards speed and sound, a little silence is not a waste of time but a way to hear oneself think.

The word 'drowned' as used in the passage means

options.A: covered up and made impossible to hear

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The sentence says 'A thought that would have been drowned by noise in the city comes forward calmly'. The noise hides the thought, so 'drowned' means covered up and made impossible to hear. Shortcut: when a word is used figuratively, choose the meaning that fits the sentence, not the dictionary's first meaning. Trap (B): Out-of-scope: this is the literal meaning, which does not fit a thought in the city. Trap (C): Reversal: the passage says that noise hides the thought. Trap (D): Out-of-scope: nothing in the sentence is about repetition.

questions.concept_tag: Factual Passage - purpose of an example
questions.question_text:
Passage: Public parks are often described as the lungs of a city, but they are much more than that. A park offers shade in the hot months and cool air in the evenings, which makes the neighbourhood around it more comfortable to live in. Trees take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen, and their leaves catch dust that would otherwise float in the air. A park is also one of the few places in a crowded town where people of different ages and incomes mix freely. Old men gather on benches to talk about the news, children play on swings, and young people jog along the paths in the morning. For families who live in small flats, the park is the only place where a child can run, kick a ball and learn how to play with others. On weekends the same paths are filled with families carrying picnic baskets, and the lawns hold impromptu games of cricket. Some parks also host morning yoga groups and evening laughter clubs, which turn a patch of grass into a small community. Studies suggest that even a short walk among trees can help people feel calmer and less tired. Despite all this, parks are often among the first places to be built over when land becomes expensive. The loss is not always noticed at once, since a building looks like progress. But the cost shows later in the form of hotter streets, more pollution and neighbourhoods where people seldom meet. A city that cares for its parks is investing in the health and happiness of the people who live in it.

The writer mentions old men, children and joggers in order to show that

options.A: only the young benefit from parks
options.B: parks are noisy and crowded places
options.C: jogging is the best use of a park
options.D: a park serves people of many ages

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The writer says a park is one of the few places where people of different ages and incomes mix freely, and gives the examples of old men, children and joggers. The examples show that a park serves people of many ages. Shortcut: ask what point the example supports; it is usually stated in the sentence just before it. Trap (A): Reversal: the examples include the old as well. Trap (B): Out-of-scope: the writer does not complain about noise or crowds. Trap (C): Extreme scope: the writer does not rank the uses of the park.

questions.concept_tag: Narrative Passage - character inference
questions.question_text:
Passage: Every evening, Mrs. D'Souza walked to the end of her lane to feed the stray dogs. She carried a steel bowl, a bottle of water and a small bag of biscuits. The neighbours had mixed feelings about this habit. Some thought it was kind; others complained that the dogs barked at night and left the road dirty. Mrs. D'Souza heard these remarks but never argued. The dogs knew her step and waited at the corner, their tails moving slowly. She had been feeding them for six years, ever since a small brown puppy had followed her home from the market. She would simply smile, nod and continue her walk. One monsoon night, a thunderstorm knocked out the lights in the whole lane. In the darkness, a small child from the next building wandered out of the gate while his parents were searching for a candle. He slipped on the wet path and began to cry. Before anyone could reach him, a group of dogs gathered around him and started to bark loudly. The noise drew the attention of the neighbours, who ran out with torches and found the boy, frightened but unhurt, sitting among the animals. The dogs had not left him alone for a moment. The next evening, nobody complained. A few people even came to the end of the lane with bowls of their own. Mrs. D'Souza said nothing about the matter; she only filled her bottle with water, as usual, and walked on. It seemed to her that kindness did not need to be defended, only to be practised.

Which of the following is true of Mrs. D'Souza?

options.A: She continued her habit calmly even when people complained.
options.B: She argued with the neighbours who complained.
options.C: She was afraid of the stray dogs.
options.D: She asked the neighbours to bring bowls.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says she heard the remarks 'but never argued', would smile and continue, and kept the same habit after the incident. She continued her habit calmly even when people complained. Shortcut: check each option against a specific sentence; the wrong ones contradict or add to the text. Trap (B): Reversal: the passage says she never argued. Trap (C): Reversal: she fed them every evening. Trap (D): Out-of-scope: the neighbours brought bowls on their own.

questions.concept_tag: Factual Passage - main idea
questions.question_text:
Passage: Learning a second language changes the way a person thinks about his own. A child who has grown up speaking only one language usually takes its rules for granted, much as we take the air we breathe for granted. When he begins to study another, he starts to see differences: a word that has no exact match, a sentence order that surprises him, a sound that does not exist in his mother tongue. These small discoveries make him more aware of how language works. Researchers have also found that people who speak two languages are often good at switching quickly between tasks and at ignoring things that distract them, perhaps because their minds are used to choosing the right language at the right moment. Learning another language can also change the way a person sees other people. Words carry the habits and humour of those who speak them, and studying them is a way of meeting a culture, not only reading about it.  Travelling becomes more rewarding as well, because a few words of the local language often open doors that remain closed to a silent visitor. None of this means that the task is easy. Pronunciation takes patience, and memory plays tricks on every learner. Mistakes are bound to happen, and they are an essential part of the process. But the reward is a mind that is flexible and curious, ready to look at familiar things from a new angle. The student who stays with it will discover that he has gained not just a new set of words, but a wider view of the world.

What is the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Children should never learn their mother tongue first.
options.B: Learning another language brings mental and cultural benefits despite the effort it requires.
options.C: Learning a second language is easy for everyone.
options.D: Mistakes show that a person should stop learning.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage lists benefits such as awareness of language, mental flexibility and cultural understanding, and admits that the task is not easy. So the main idea is that learning another language brings mental and cultural benefits despite the effort. Shortcut: a main-idea option should cover both the benefits and the difficulty mentioned. Trap (A): Out-of-scope: the passage gives no such advice. Trap (C): Reversal: the passage says the task is not easy. Trap (D): Reversal: mistakes are called an essential part of the process.

questions.concept_tag: Factual Passage - tone and purpose
questions.question_text:
Passage: Clean drinking water is something most of us rarely think about, until the tap runs dry. In many parts of the world, women and children walk for hours every day to bring a few buckets of water to their homes. This time cannot be used for school or for work, and the water that they carry is often not safe to drink. Illnesses that spread through dirty water keep children away from classrooms and families away from their jobs. Solving the problem does not always require expensive machines. In some villages, a simple well with a covered top and a hand pump has changed daily life within a few months. In others, a community has agreed to keep the stream above the village free of waste, so that the water downstream remains fit to use. The success of such efforts nearly always depends on the people themselves. A pump that is installed without their agreement may be left to rust, whereas a pump that the village has helped to choose, pay for and maintain is more likely to last.  In one district, a group of women even trained as pump mechanics, and their repairs kept the machines working for years. Governments and organisations can provide funds and training, but ownership has to remain with those who use the water every day. This is a lesson that applies far beyond water. Help that is offered with respect, and shared with the people it is meant to serve, tends to last longer than help that is simply delivered.

The passage suggests that water projects succeed mainly when

options.A: they use the most expensive machines
options.B: they are managed only by outside experts
options.C: the villagers take part in and look after them
options.D: water is carried over long distances

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says that success nearly always depends on the people themselves, and that a pump the village helped to choose, pay for and maintain is more likely to last. So projects succeed when villagers take part in them and look after them. Shortcut: find the sentence with 'depends on' or 'success': it states the condition asked about. Trap (A): Reversal: the passage says simple solutions can work. Trap (B): Reversal: the passage says ownership must remain with the users. Trap (D): Out-of-scope: long walks are described as part of the problem, not the solution.

questions.concept_tag: Discursive Passage - writer's view of translation
questions.question_text:
Passage: A translator is often described as a bridge between two languages, but the picture is too simple. A bridge carries a traveller unchanged from one bank to the other, whereas a translation always changes something on the way. Words rarely have exact twins in another language. The Hindi word for a particular relation, such as a mother's younger brother, may need a whole phrase in English, while an English word such as 'privacy' may have no single partner in many other languages. A joke, in particular, rarely survives the journey, because its humour often depends on the sound of a word. Even when a close match exists, it may carry a different shade of feeling: a word that sounds affectionate in one language may seem formal or even cold in another. Poetry presents the hardest challenge, because the sound, rhythm and meaning of a line are bound together, and a translator cannot keep all three at once. Some choose to remain close to the original words and accept that the result will sound strange; others write a new poem that follows the spirit of the original but changes its details. Neither choice is wrong, and readers disagree about which is better. What the best translators share is humility. They know that they will lose something, and so they work with great care to decide what is worth saving. Readers who understand this do not treat a translation as a perfect copy. They treat it as an invitation, a way into a world that they would otherwise never enter, and they remain curious about the original that stands behind it.

Which of the following best reflects the writer's view of translation?

options.A: It is impossible, so readers should not rely on translations.
options.B: A translator should always stay as close as possible to the original words.
options.C: It always involves choices and some loss, yet it has real value for readers.
options.D: A good translation is a perfect copy of the original.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The writer rejects the bridge image because translation changes things, describes what is lost, says that neither approach to poetry is wrong, and ends by calling a translation an invitation. So the view is that translation always involves choices and loss, yet is valuable. Shortcut: for a view question, collect the writer's claims from the beginning and the end, and choose the option that fits all of them. Trap (A): Extreme scope: the writer calls translation an invitation into a new world, not something to avoid. Trap (B): Half-true: this is one choice the writer mentions, but the writer says neither choice is wrong. Trap (D): Reversal: the writer says readers should not treat a translation as a perfect copy.

questions.concept_tag: Discursive Passage - reason for an effect
questions.question_text:
Passage: Schools in many countries have begun to give less time to handwriting, since children are expected to type most of their work in later life. The change seems sensible: typing is faster, the result is easier to read, and mistakes can be corrected without crossing anything out. Many parents welcome the change, since they see their children spend hours practising letters that a screen will soon replace. Yet some researchers urge caution. In several small studies, students who took notes by hand were found to remember the ideas of a lecture better than those who typed. One explanation is that handwriting is slow, so the writer cannot copy everything and must decide what to keep. This act of choosing and rephrasing helps the mind to understand the material. A student at a keyboard, by contrast, often copies the words almost without thought and finds, later, that little has remained in memory. The studies do not prove that typing is harmful, and the researchers themselves warn that the results may differ with age, subject and the type of test. Nor do they suggest that computers should be removed from the classroom. A more modest conclusion is that the two methods may serve different purposes: the keyboard for speed, length and editing, and the pen for thinking through something new. Teachers could therefore ask their students to use both, with notes by hand during a lesson and the final essay at the screen. The aim would not be to defend an old skill out of sentiment, but to use each tool where it works best.

According to the passage, why might notes taken by hand help students remember better?

options.A: The writer has to select and rephrase ideas instead of copying them.
options.B: Handwriting is faster than typing, so more can be noted.
options.C: Pens are less distracting than computers.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says that 'handwriting is slow, so the writer cannot copy everything and must decide what to keep', and that choosing and rephrasing helps the mind understand. This is the reason given. Shortcut: find the sentence introducing 'one explanation' and read the reason it gives. Trap (B): Reversal: the passage says handwriting is slow, which is the reason for the effect. Trap (C): Out-of-scope: distraction is not mentioned as a reason. Trap (D): Half-true: the passage says typing makes correction easy, not that handwriting is free of errors.

questions.concept_tag: Narrative Passage - reading emotion from behaviour
questions.question_text:
Passage: For thirty years Anand had tended the lamp at the end of the headland, and in all that time he had spoken to perhaps two hundred people. The fishermen who passed in their boats raised a hand to him, and he returned the gesture, but his life was made of routine: trimming the wick in the old days, then checking the machinery when the electric light replaced it, writing the weather in a thick register each dusk. When the authorities decided to make the lighthouse fully automatic, a young engineer arrived to explain the new system. Anand listened politely and nodded at the right moments. The young man spoke quickly and used words that Anand did not know, but he was kind enough to repeat himself twice. He did not argue, for he had always believed that machines did their work without sentiment. On the last evening, he climbed the stairs, one hundred and twelve in number, and stood beside the great lens as the lamp came on. Out at sea, the first boat turned towards the harbour, guided by the beam. Anand had seen the same sight ten thousand times, yet that evening his hands trembled. He realised that the light had never been merely a machine to him; it had been the one promise that he had made to strangers whom he would never meet. In the morning, he handed the keys to the engineer, shook his hand, and walked down the path without looking back. Those who saw him go said that he seemed lighter, though nobody could say why.

Why did Anand's hands tremble on the last evening?

options.A: He was afraid of the new machinery.
options.B: He was angry with the young engineer.
options.C: He was cold from the wind at sea.
options.D: He suddenly understood how much the work had meant to him.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says that on the last evening 'he realised that the light had never been merely a machine to him; it had been the one promise that he had made to strangers'. The trembling comes with this realisation of the meaning of his work. Shortcut: link the physical sign (trembling) with the sentence that follows it, which gives the reason. Trap (A): Out-of-scope: his fear of machines is never mentioned; he listened politely. Trap (B): Reversal: he shook the engineer's hand at the end. Trap (C): Out-of-scope: the weather is not given as the cause.

questions.concept_tag: Factual Passage - cause behind a limit
questions.question_text:
Passage: Some harmless butterflies survive because they look like dangerous ones. This trick, known as mimicry, is common in the insect world. Certain butterflies feed on plants that make them taste bitter or even poisonous, and birds that have once eaten one learn to avoid its bright colours. A second species that is perfectly tasty may then evolve a similar pattern of colours and so gain protection without the need to be poisonous itself. Naturalists first described this kind of copying more than a century ago after collecting butterflies in a tropical forest. The imitation is sometimes so close that even a trained collector can be misled. The system, however, has a weak point. If the copies become too common compared with the poisonous species, young birds will often eat a tasty copy and find it pleasant, and the warning colours lose their meaning. For this reason, mimics tend to remain fewer in number than the species that they imitate. Scientists have also noticed that some poisonous species resemble one another, forming 'clubs' in which several bitter-tasting kinds share the same colours. In this case, the benefit is mutual: a predator needs to taste only one member of the club in order to avoid all of them, and so fewer individuals of each kind are lost during the lessons. Mimicry shows that appearance can be as useful as chemistry in the struggle to survive. It also illustrates the way in which natural selection works through small advantages repeated over many generations, until an elaborate pattern that no butterfly planned becomes part of the species.

According to the passage, why do mimics usually remain fewer in number than the species they copy?

options.A: The poisonous butterflies drive them away.
options.B: If they became too common, birds would learn that the pattern does not mean a bad taste.
options.C: Birds prefer to eat bitter butterflies.
options.D: They cannot find enough food plants.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says that when copies become too common, young birds eat a tasty copy and find it pleasant, so the warning colours lose their meaning; hence mimics stay fewer than the species they imitate. Shortcut: look for 'for this reason' in the passage, and read the sentence before it for the cause. Trap (A): Out-of-scope: no hostility between the two kinds is mentioned. Trap (C): Reversal: birds avoid the bitter ones and are happy to find a tasty copy. Trap (D): Out-of-scope: food plants are mentioned only for the poisonous kind.

questions.concept_tag: Factual Passage - statement not supported (EXCEPT)
questions.question_text:
Passage: Most of the great cities of the ancient world grew beside rivers, and the reasons are not hard to find. A river provided drinking water and made the surrounding soil rich with silt, so that farmers could grow more food than their own families needed. The surplus allowed some people to leave the fields and become potters, traders, builders or priests, and in this way a village slowly became a town. Such a change took many generations, and the people who lived through it would hardly have noticed it happening. Rivers also offered the cheapest road of the time. Boats could carry heavy loads of grain, timber and stone over long distances at a fraction of the effort needed to drag them across land. Towns on the banks could therefore trade with distant places and receive new ideas along with new goods. Yet the river that gave life could also take it away. Floods could destroy fields and houses, and an unexpected change in the course of the stream could leave a thriving port far from the water. Cities responded by building embankments, canals and storehouses, and these projects demanded planning and cooperation on a large scale. Some historians therefore argue that the need to manage rivers helped to create the first organised governments. This view is attractive, but it is not accepted by everyone. Others point out that some early cities developed without large irrigation works, and that rivers alone cannot explain the rise of urban life. The truth probably lies in a combination of many causes, of which the river was one of the most important.

Which one of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage?

options.A: Rivers helped farmers to grow more food than their families needed.
options.B: All historians agree that river management led to the first organised governments.
options.C: Boats were a cheap way to carry heavy goods.
options.D: Floods were a danger to river cities.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says that some historians hold the view about governments, but 'it is not accepted by everyone'. So the claim that all historians agree is not supported. The other three statements appear directly in the passage. Shortcut: in an EXCEPT or NOT question, check each option against the passage and look for words like 'all' that go beyond the text. Trap (A): This is supported: the passage says rich silt allowed a surplus, so it cannot be the answer. Trap (C): This is supported: boats carried loads at a fraction of the effort of dragging them over land. Trap (D): This is supported: floods could destroy fields and houses.

questions.concept_tag: Cultural Passage - writer's main concern
questions.question_text:
Passage: Folk songs are often described as the memory of a community, and the description is truer than it first appears. Before schools and books reached every village, a song was one of the few ways in which a people could keep its history. A harvest song carried knowledge of the seasons, a lullaby preserved a family's customs, and a ballad about a local hero told the young what their elders valued. Grandmothers sang while grinding grain, and children learned the words without ever being taught them. Because these songs were passed from mouth to mouth, they were never fixed. Each singer made small changes, forgetting a line, adding a name or fitting the tune to a new occasion. A traveller might hear a song at one wedding and a slightly different version at the next. Scholars who collect folk songs today are often surprised to find several versions of the same song in neighbouring villages, each version slightly different, and each insisting that it is the true one. This variety is not a defect, but a sign of life. A song that nobody changes is a song that nobody sings. The danger today is not that songs change, but that they are no longer sung at all. As people move to cities and listen to recorded music, the old songs are heard less often, and many are known only by a few elderly singers. Collecting them is therefore urgent work. But recordings alone cannot save a tradition. A song survives when it is used, at a wedding, in a field or around a fire, and not when it lies silent in an archive.

What is the writer's main concern in the passage?

options.A: Folk songs should be kept exactly as they were first sung.
options.B: Recorded music is of poor quality.
options.C: Scholars have found only one version of each song.
options.D: Folk songs may vanish if they stop being sung in everyday life.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The writer says that the danger is not that songs change but that they are no longer sung, and that a song survives when it is used, not when it lies in an archive. So the main concern is that folk songs may vanish if they stop being sung in everyday life. Shortcut: the concern is usually stated near the end after words like 'the danger' or 'the problem'. Trap (A): Reversal: the writer says variety is a sign of life. Trap (B): Out-of-scope: the quality of recordings is not discussed. Trap (C): Reversal: they find several versions in neighbouring villages.

questions.concept_tag: Discursive Passage - purpose of an example
questions.question_text:
Passage: An average can be a useful summary, but it can also mislead. Suppose a news report states that the average income in a small town is a high figure. A visitor might imagine a prosperous place, with comfortable homes and well-paid workers. Yet the average could be raised greatly by a single rich businessman living among hundreds of ordinary families. In this case, the figure describes almost nobody. The same thing happens when a few very large farms raise the average size of land holdings in a district. Statisticians therefore often prefer to use the median, the middle value when all incomes are arranged in order, which is not affected by one extreme case. For this reason, official reports on incomes often quote the median alongside the average. Even the median hides details, however. It does not tell us whether the incomes are close together or widely spread, nor how many families live below an acceptable standard. An average also says nothing about the way in which a quantity changes over time or differs from one place to another. A city may have a mild average temperature across the year and still have scorching summers and freezing winters that make life difficult. None of this means that averages are useless. It means that a number should be read together with the question it is meant to answer. A careful reader asks how the figure was calculated, who was included, and what was left out. Without such questions, a single number may create a false impression of precision. With them, it becomes one of the most helpful tools for understanding a complicated world.

The writer mentions a city with a mild average temperature in order to show that

options.A: an average can hide large differences within the data.
options.B: cities with mild averages are always comfortable to live in.
options.C: temperature is a more important figure than income.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The writer says an average 'says nothing about the way in which a quantity changes' and gives the example of a city with a mild yearly average but extreme summers and winters. The example shows that an average can hide large differences. Shortcut: ask what point the example supports; the sentences before and after it state the point. Trap (B): Reversal: the example shows that such a city may still have scorching summers and freezing winters. Trap (C): Out-of-scope: no ranking of kinds of data is made. Trap (D): Extreme scope: the writer says averages are useful and not useless.

questions.concept_tag: Policy Passage - main argument
questions.question_text:
Passage: When a city builds a new road to relieve traffic, the relief rarely lasts. Drivers who had avoided a crowded route now return to it, others move to the suburbs that the road has made easier to reach, and within a few years the new lanes are as full as the old ones. Anyone who has watched a widened highway fill up again will recognise the pattern. Transport planners call this the problem of induced demand: the supply of road space creates its own demand. A growing number of cities have therefore turned to a different strategy. Instead of making it easier to drive, they make it easier to travel without a car. They add frequent buses, protect bicycle lanes and place stations close to housing, markets and schools. The results are not instant, and car owners often complain that their journeys have been made harder. But the evidence suggests that when a service is reliable and convenient, many people will choose it, even if they own a car. The change also saves money. A single train carrying a large number of passengers needs far less space than the same number of people in separate cars, and the land that is saved can be used for parks or homes. Critics reply that such systems are costly to build and that some people, such as those who carry heavy tools or live in distant villages, will always need cars. These objections deserve attention. They do not, however, weaken the main lesson, which is that a city cannot build its way out of congestion by making driving ever easier.

Which of the following best states the main argument of the passage?

options.A: Cars should be banned from all cities.
options.B: Public transport systems are cheap to build.
options.C: Cities should improve alternatives to the car, since new roads do not solve congestion for long.
options.D: New roads never reduce traffic even for a day.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage explains induced demand, describes cities that favour buses, bicycles and stations, notes objections, and concludes that a city cannot build its way out of congestion by making driving easier. So the main argument is to improve alternatives, since new roads do not solve congestion for long. Shortcut: the last sentence often carries the main lesson; check that it fits the option. Trap (A): Extreme scope: the writer admits that some people will always need cars. Trap (B): Reversal: critics say they are costly, and the writer does not deny it. Trap (D): Extreme scope: the passage says the relief rarely lasts, not that it never occurs.

questions.concept_tag: Reflective Passage - vocabulary in context
questions.question_text:
Passage: A reader of a hundred years ago would probably be surprised by the way we read today. We scan headlines, skim emails and jump from one page to another within seconds. Even a long novel is sometimes read in short bursts between messages. Reading has become a way of collecting information as quickly as possible. There is nothing wrong with this; much of what we read, such as a timetable or a notice, deserves no more than a glance. But a quick glance cannot take the place of slow reading, in which a person stays with a text, rereads a difficult sentence and allows the meaning to settle. Slow reading is not simply reading at a lower speed. It is a way of paying attention that lets the reader notice the choice of a word, the rhythm of a sentence or a quiet contradiction in the argument. Such attention is needed for any writing that tries to say something new or complex. Because it requires effort, it is easily lost; a mind used to constant interruption finds it hard to remain with a single page. Some teachers now set aside a short period each day in which students read a chosen book in silence, with no phones and no discussion. At first, the students are restless, but after a few weeks many say they are able to read for longer and understand more. The lesson is not that fast reading is bad, but that we need both kinds, and that the slow kind will not grow unless we protect the time in which it can happen.

The word 'settle' in the passage most nearly means

options.A: become clear and steady in the mind
options.B: sink to the bottom of a liquid

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The sentence says that the reader 'rereads a difficult sentence and allows the meaning to settle'. The meaning is not ending or sinking; it becomes clear and steady in the mind as the reader stays with it. Shortcut: substitute each option in the sentence and test which one keeps the sense of the whole passage. Trap (B): Out-of-scope: this is the literal meaning, which does not suit 'meaning'. Trap (C): Out-of-scope: this is an unrelated use of the word. Trap (D): Half-true: it suggests finishing, but the sentence is about understanding that grows, not ending.

questions.concept_tag: Discursive Passage - writer's attitude
questions.question_text:
Passage: Visitors to a museum are sometimes disappointed to learn that the statue in front of them is a copy. They feel that they have been cheated of the real thing. Some even ask for their money back. The museum, however, may have excellent reasons for the substitution. An original stone figure, after centuries in the open air, may have grown so fragile that wind, rain or even the breath of crowds would damage it further. Moving it indoors preserves it, while a careful replica in its original place allows the public to enjoy the design as the artist intended. Replicas are also useful in other ways. A cast can be taken to schools and villages that will never see the original, and students can touch it, which would never be allowed with the real object. For researchers, a copy that records every scratch and crack serves as a permanent record, should the original be lost or damaged. Still, replicas cannot replace the original in every respect. The surface of an ancient object carries the marks of its age and use, and many visitors say that standing close to such an object gives them a feeling that no copy can create. This feeling is hard to measure, but it is genuine, and museums would be unwise to dismiss it. The best policy is probably an honest one: to display copies where needed, to label them clearly and to explain why the choice was made, so that visitors may understand that a copy can serve a purpose without pretending to be what it is not.

The writer's attitude towards museum replicas is best described as

options.C: balanced and appreciative of their uses

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The writer defends replicas (protection, teaching, research) and also admits their limits and the genuine feeling given by originals, and recommends honest labelling. The attitude is balanced and appreciative. Shortcut: for attitude questions, note praise and criticism together; a balanced passage rarely has an extreme attitude. Trap (A): Reversal: the writer lists their many uses. Trap (B): Extreme scope: the writer says that replicas cannot replace the original in every respect. Trap (D): Reversal: the writer says that museums would be unwise to dismiss visitors' feelings.

questions.concept_tag: Literary Passage - interpretation of an event
questions.question_text:
Passage: Mukund sat at the wheel before dawn, as he had done since he was twelve. The clay had to be wedged, folded and pressed again and again until no air remained in it; otherwise, he knew, the pot would crack in the fire. His father had taught him this, and had also taught him to keep his hands wet and his eyes on the centre. 'The wheel does not forgive a wandering mind,' he used to say. The village had known three generations of potters from that family, and the courtyard was lined with old, cracked pots that he had never thrown away. Today, however, Mukund's mind wandered. His daughter had written from the city that she wished to become an engineer, and that she did not intend to return to the village. He was proud of her, but he could not stop thinking about the empty seat at the wheel. As he thought, the clay in his hands began to lean and wobble, and within a moment the half-formed pot collapsed. He looked at the shapeless mass for some time. Then, instead of throwing it into the waste pit, he gathered it, pressed it back into a ball and set it again at the centre of the wheel. This time his fingers were steady. By the time the sun lit the courtyard, a small round pot stood on the board, plain but true. Mukund wiped his hands slowly. It occurred to him that one could not make another person's life on any wheel, only the pot in front of oneself, and that the second attempt was often the better one.

What does the collapse and remaking of the pot suggest about Mukund?

options.A: He decides to stop making pots.
options.B: He blames his father's teaching for the failure.
options.C: He is angry with his daughter for leaving.
options.D: He accepts that his daughter's path is her own and regains his calm.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Mukund's mind wanders because of his daughter's plans; the pot collapses. He remakes it with steady hands, and realises that one cannot make another person's life, only one's own work. So he accepts her path and regains calm. Shortcut: treat the failure and recovery of the task as a symbol of the character's inner change. Trap (A): Out-of-scope: he sets the clay again and finishes a pot. Trap (B): Reversal: the father's advice about a wandering mind is shown to be true. Trap (C): Reversal: the passage says that he was proud of her.

questions.concept_tag: Factual Passage - cause of an effect
questions.question_text:
Passage: The rise and fall of the sea twice a day has been noticed by sailors for thousands of years, but its cause was understood only gradually. The main reason is the pull of the moon. The moon's gravity attracts the water on the side of the earth nearest to it and raises a bulge there. At the same time, a second bulge forms on the opposite side of the planet, and as the earth turns, any given coast passes through both bulges each day. Most coasts therefore see two high tides and two low tides in a little more than a day. The sun also pulls on the sea, although its effect is smaller because it is much farther away. When the sun, earth and moon lie in a straight line, as they do at new moon and full moon, their pulls combine, and the tides are especially high and low. When the sun and moon pull at right angles, as at the quarter moons, their effects partly cancel, and the tides are moderate. The shape of the coast makes a great difference too. In a wide, open bay the water may rise only a little, while in a narrow funnel-shaped inlet it can be forced upwards to a great height. Fishermen and harbour pilots have always planned their work according to the tides, and today tide tables are printed well in advance because the motions of the moon and sun can be calculated with great accuracy. Yet the sea itself remains unpredictable in other ways, and a storm can raise the water far beyond the level in any table.

According to the passage, why are the tides especially high and low at new moon and full moon?

options.A: The moon is closest to the earth at those times.
options.B: The pulls of the sun and the moon act together.
options.C: The sun and moon pull at right angles at those times.
options.D: The coast is narrower at those times.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says: 'When the sun, earth and moon lie in a straight line, as they do at new moon and full moon, their pulls combine, and the tides are especially high and low.' Shortcut: find 'new moon and full moon' in the passage and read the cause given in the same sentence. Trap (A): Out-of-scope: the passage does not mention the moon's distance. Trap (C): Reversal: this happens at the quarter moons, giving moderate tides. Trap (D): Out-of-scope: the shape of the coast does not change with the moon's phase.

questions.concept_tag: Discursive Passage - inference
questions.question_text:
Passage: A student who has just failed an experiment often feels that nothing has been achieved. The result is not what the textbook promised, the report cannot be written as planned and the teacher may be disappointed. The student's classmates, whose experiments worked, seem to have moved ahead. Yet the history of science suggests that failure is not the opposite of discovery, but a regular part of it. Many important findings came about when an experiment did not go as expected. A researcher who notices an odd result, instead of throwing it away, may open a new line of enquiry. This requires a certain attitude: the readiness to ask whether the unexpected result is a mistake in the method or a hint about the world. To tell the difference, scientists repeat the experiment, change a single factor at a time and keep careful records. This slow, patient routine is rarely mentioned in popular accounts of great discoveries, which prefer sudden flashes of insight. A failure that is recorded honestly is therefore useful to others, who can avoid the same path or try a different one. Unfortunately, journals tend to publish successful results far more readily than failed ones. As a result, other researchers may spend months repeating an attempt that has already failed elsewhere. Some scientists now argue that negative results should be shared more openly. For students, the lesson is simple. A failed experiment should not be hidden or forgotten. It should be examined with the same care as a success, because it may contain information that the planned result could never have given.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: Scientists should avoid experiments that might fail.
options.C: Every failed experiment leads to a new discovery.
options.D: Failed experiments that are not reported may lead other researchers to waste effort.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says journals prefer successful results, so other researchers may repeat an attempt that has already failed. It follows that unreported failures can lead others to waste effort. Shortcut: an inference must follow from a cause-and-effect statement in the passage, without 'always' or 'every'. Trap (A): Reversal: the passage treats failure as a regular part of discovery. Trap (B): Reversal: journals publish successful results more readily. Trap (C): Extreme scope: the passage says failure may open a line of enquiry, not that it always does.

questions.concept_tag: Discursive Passage - implied view
questions.question_text:
Passage: Fashion changes with the seasons, and the pace has grown faster in recent decades. Clothes that are cheap to buy are often cheap to make, and many are worn only a few times before they are thrown away. A shirt that costs less than a meal may be discarded after a single season, simply because it is out of fashion. The cost of this habit is not seen at the shop counter. Producing cloth uses large amounts of water and energy, and the dyes used to colour it may pollute rivers near factories. Discarded garments fill landfills, where synthetic fibres may remain for a very long time. Some shoppers respond by buying fewer clothes of better quality, and by repairing what they own instead of replacing it. Others borrow, swap or buy second-hand, so that a garment passes through several owners before its life ends. Such habits are not new. In earlier times, a coat was altered for a younger sibling and the leftover cloth was used for patches or cleaning rags. What has changed is the speed at which fashion is sold and the pressure to look new. Reducing waste does not mean giving up style. A person who chooses carefully, wears things for years and mends them with skill may express more individuality than one who simply follows each new trend. Producers have a responsibility too: they can design clothes to last, use fabrics that can be recycled, and be open about how their goods are made. But in the end, the decision to buy or not to buy rests with each of us.

The writer suggests that reducing clothing waste

options.A: requires people to wear only plain clothes
options.B: is the duty of producers alone
options.C: is compatible with having a personal style
options.D: was a practice unknown to earlier generations

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The writer says that 'Reducing waste does not mean giving up style' and that careful buyers may show more individuality. So reducing waste is compatible with personal style. Shortcut: check each option against the sentence that begins with 'Reducing waste does not mean'. Trap (A): Reversal: the writer says that reducing waste does not mean giving up style. Trap (B): Extreme scope: the writer says that producers have a responsibility too, and that the decision rests with each of us. Trap (D): Reversal: the writer says that such habits are not new.

questions.concept_tag: Balanced Passage - agreement with the writer
questions.question_text:
Passage: Every year, many villagers leave their homes and move to cities in the hope of finding work. Their reasons are easy to understand. A farm that has been divided among several sons may be too small to support them all, and a poor harvest can leave a family in debt. In some districts, the young men have no wish to spend their lives behind a plough as their fathers did. The city offers wages, schools and hospitals that the village may lack. Yet the move is rarely simple. Newcomers often live in crowded rooms, work long hours at low pay and send most of their earnings home. They may feel lonely among strangers, and the language, food and customs of the city may seem unfamiliar. Back in the village, those who stay behind face problems of their own. When young men leave, the old and the women must carry out the heavy work of the fields, and some villages become so thin in population that schools and shops close. At the same time, the money that migrants send home can pay for medicines, a new roof or a younger brother's school fees, and some of them return with skills that help to improve local farming or open small businesses. Whether migration is a gain or a loss for a village therefore depends on many things: how many leave, who they are, and whether they come back. The question cannot be answered with a simple yes or no, and policies which treat migrants only as a problem, or only as a solution, are likely to fail.

With which of the following statements would the writer be most likely to agree?

options.A: Policies on migration should take both its benefits and its costs into account.
options.B: Villages are better off when most young people leave.
options.C: Migrants should be discouraged from sending money home.
options.D: Migrants face no difficulties in the city.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The writer says the effect depends on many things and that policies treating migrants only as a problem or only as a solution will fail. So the writer would agree that policies should consider both benefits and costs. Shortcut: the final sentence usually gives the writer's recommendation. Trap (B): Extreme scope: the writer notes that schools and shops may close when too many leave. Trap (C): Out-of-scope: the passage values the money that is sent home. Trap (D): Reversal: the passage lists crowded rooms, long hours and loneliness.

questions.concept_tag: Discursive Passage - statement not true (NOT)
questions.question_text:
Passage: A teacher who makes his class laugh is sometimes suspected of wasting time. Serious learning, it is said, needs serious faces. But the evidence from classrooms does not support such a view. Many students can recall a lesson mainly because of a single funny remark made by the teacher. A well-chosen joke can wake up a tired class, and a funny example can help a student to remember a rule that would otherwise be forgotten. Humour also changes the atmosphere. A student who is afraid of being laughed at will often avoid asking a question, whereas one who has seen the teacher laugh at his own mistakes feels freer to speak. Laughter, after all, has a way of relaxing the shoulders and loosening the tongue. This does not mean that every kind of humour is helpful. Jokes that make fun of a particular student, of a person's accent or of a group of people hurt and silence the very pupils the teacher hopes to reach. Nor should humour become a performance in which the teacher's wit matters more than the lesson. The best use of laughter is gentle and connected to the subject, such as an absurd example in a maths problem or a play on words in a grammar lesson. It also requires an alert teacher who can tell when the mood has changed, and the class is ready to become serious again. Used in this way, humour is not a distraction from learning but one of the quiet means by which a classroom becomes a place where people feel safe enough to think aloud.

According to the passage, which of the following uses of humour is NOT helpful in a classroom?

options.A: A funny example in a maths problem
options.B: Jokes that make fun of a particular student
options.C: A play on words in a grammar lesson
options.D: A teacher laughing at his own mistakes

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage warns that jokes that make fun of a particular student, an accent or a group hurt and silence pupils. The other three uses are described as helpful. Shortcut: in a NOT question, mark which options are supported and pick the one that is warned against. Trap (A): This is helpful according to the passage, so it cannot be the answer. Trap (C): This is helpful according to the passage, so it cannot be the answer. Trap (D): This is helpful according to the passage: it helps students to speak freely, so it cannot be the answer.

questions.concept_tag: Factual Passage - reason for reliability
questions.question_text:
Passage: Every autumn, millions of birds leave their summer homes and travel thousands of kilometres to warmer regions, and every spring they return, often to the very same tree. The journey may take weeks, with stops to rest and feed along the way. How do they find their way? Scientists have found that birds use not one method but several. Different species rely on different combinations, depending on when and where they fly. During the day, many of them judge direction from the position of the sun and correct for its movement across the sky. At night, some species use the pattern of the stars; young birds raised under an artificial sky have been shown to learn the patterns that surround the point where the stars appear to turn. Birds also appear to sense the earth's magnetic field, which acts like a faint compass built into the body, although exactly how they do so is still not fully understood. In addition, landmarks such as rivers, coastlines and mountain ranges help them to follow a route that they have flown before, and a few species are thought to recognise scents carried on the wind. When one method fails, perhaps because of cloud, the birds can switch to another. This flexibility may explain why migration is so reliable despite the many dangers on the way. Yet the system is not perfect. Bright city lights can confuse night travellers, and storms may blow them far off course. The remarkable feat of migration thus rests on a delicate combination of senses, and it can be disturbed when any of them is interfered with.

According to the passage, what may explain why bird migration is so reliable?

options.A: Birds travel only on days when the sky is clear.
options.B: Birds follow a single fixed star all the way.
options.C: Birds can use several methods of navigation and switch when one fails.
options.D: Scientists have fully understood the magnetic sense.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says: 'When one method fails, perhaps because of cloud, the birds can switch to another. This flexibility may explain why migration is so reliable.' Shortcut: find the phrase 'may explain' and read the sentence just before it. Trap (A): Reversal: birds can switch methods when cloud blocks one of them. Trap (B): Half-true: some use the stars, but not a single one, and they use other methods as well. Trap (D): Reversal: the passage says that how birds sense the field is still not fully understood.

questions.concept_tag: Reflective Passage - meaning of a phrase
questions.question_text:
Passage: My grandmother never owned a measuring cup, yet her cooking was never the same twice and never anything but good. She worked by feel, by smell and by sound, and she regarded a recipe as a rough idea rather than a law. Her kitchen was small, with a single stove, two blackened pans and a shelf of unlabelled jars whose contents she could name by smell alone. 'The pot will tell you,' she used to say, lifting the lid to listen to the bubbling. As a child, I thought this was magic. Guests who tasted her food would ask for the recipe, and she would laugh and say that there was none. Later, when I studied science, I began to see her kitchen as a laboratory. When she let the onions cook until they were golden, she was changing the sugars in them; when she rested the dough in a warm corner, she was giving the yeast time to make gas. She knew none of these terms, but she understood the results thoroughly, and she learned it through thousands of small trials. What impressed me most was her willingness to make mistakes without distress. A curry that turned out too sour was a lesson for the next day, and nobody was scolded. Today, I follow recipes more closely than she ever did, and I measure carefully. Yet when something goes wrong, I find myself lifting the lid and listening, as she did. Perhaps this is what it means to learn from someone: not to copy the exact steps, but to take on the habit of attention that lies behind them.

What does the narrator mean by 'the habit of attention'?

options.A: Noticing carefully what is happening while one works
options.B: Measuring every ingredient with great exactness
options.C: Following a recipe step by step without change
options.D: Learning the scientific names of cooking processes

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The narrator describes the grandmother as working by feel, smell and sound, and says that she herself lifts the lid and listens when something goes wrong. So the habit of attention is careful noticing of what happens while working. Shortcut: look at the examples the writer gives just before the phrase. Trap (B): Reversal: the grandmother owned no measuring cup, and the habit is not about measurement. Trap (C): Reversal: she regarded a recipe as a rough idea. Trap (D): Out-of-scope: the narrator says she knew none of these terms.

questions.concept_tag: Discursive Passage - purpose of the writer
questions.question_text:
Passage: A false story can travel around the world while the truth is still putting on its shoes. This old saying has become more accurate in an age when a message can be shared with hundreds of people in a few seconds. A rumour that once needed weeks to cross a district now needs only an afternoon. A shocking claim, a dramatic photograph or an angry post tends to spread faster than a calm correction, partly because it provokes strong feelings, and strong feelings make us eager to pass it on. By the time the facts have been checked, the first version has often reached many more people than the correction ever will. This does not mean that everyone who shares a false story intends to deceive. Most do so out of worry, concern or simple trust in a friend. The remedy lies in small habits. Before sharing a surprising item, a reader can ask who first published it, whether other reliable sources report the same thing, and whether the photograph has been used in a different context before. These questions take only a minute. The habit is easy to learn and costs nothing. Schools can also help by teaching students how to compare sources and how to recognise language designed to alarm. Platforms and news organisations have a part to play as well, by making corrections as visible as the original claims. None of this will end rumours altogether, which are as old as human society. But a community that has learned to pause before it shares can slow a false story enough for the truth to catch up.

What is the writer's main purpose in the passage?

options.A: To prove that everyone who shares a false story means to deceive
options.B: To suggest simple habits that can slow the spread of false information
options.C: To argue that the sharing of messages should be banned
options.D: To describe how photographs are edited

questions.pedagogical_explanation: After describing how false stories spread, the writer says 'the remedy lies in small habits', lists questions readers can ask and roles for schools and platforms. The purpose is to suggest habits that can slow false information. Shortcut: identify the section that offers 'the remedy'; it shows what the writer wants to achieve. Trap (A): Reversal: the writer says that most people share out of worry, concern or trust. Trap (C): Out-of-scope: no ban is proposed. Trap (D): Out-of-scope: editing techniques are not discussed.

questions.concept_tag: Balanced Passage - best title
questions.question_text:
Passage: The slopes of a mountain valley can look like paradise to a visitor from a crowded city. The air is cool, the villages are quiet, and the view changes with every turn of the road. Small guesthouses, painted in bright colours, cling to the hillsides, and smoke rises slowly from the kitchens in the early morning. It is not surprising that tourism has grown in such places. For local families, it brings new income: they rent rooms, run small cafes and guide trekkers along the trails. Many young people who would otherwise have left for the plains are able to stay near home. Their parents, who once worried about empty houses, now plan to add another room. But the same visitors who bring money also place heavy demands on a fragile place. Water that was once enough for the village may not be enough for hotels and their guests. Paths are worn bare by thousands of feet, and rubbish left along the way takes years to disappear in the cold. Prices rise, and some local people find that they can no longer afford to live in their own village. These problems do not mean that tourism should be stopped. A more careful approach would limit the number of visitors in the busiest season, require that waste be carried down, and encourage guests to stay in homes owned by local families. Such rules can seem inconvenient, and some visitors resent them. But they protect what people come to see. A mountain that is loved to destruction is no longer a place worth visiting, and a village that cannot support its own people can hardly welcome strangers.

Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.A: Why Mountains Should Be Closed to Visitors
options.B: The Pleasures of Life in a Big City
options.C: How to Run a Successful Mountain Hotel
options.D: Tourism in the Mountains: Gains and Burdens

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage explains the benefits of mountain tourism (income, jobs) and its burdens (water, paths, prices) and proposes careful limits. The best title covers both: 'Tourism in the Mountains: Gains and Burdens'. Shortcut: a title must fit the whole passage and keep its balance. Trap (A): Reversal: the writer says that tourism should not be stopped. Trap (B): Out-of-scope: the city is mentioned only for the visitor's contrast. Trap (C): Out-of-scope: hotel management is not discussed.

questions.concept_tag: Inference - social role of stepwells
questions.question_text:
Passage: In the dry regions of western India, stepwells were built not merely to store water but to organise community life around it. A stepwell descends in flights of stone stairs to the water table, and the steps allow people to reach the water whatever the season: when the level falls after a poor monsoon, they simply walk further down. The engineering is subtle. The deep, shaded chambers stay many degrees cooler than the baking air above, and travellers who rested there found relief that a simple open well could never offer. Because women were usually the ones who fetched water, the stepwell became a place where they met, exchanged news and, in some villages, held small festivals. Carved pillars and sculpted niches suggest that builders and patrons thought of these structures as more than utilities; a well was an act of merit as well as an act of planning. When piped water arrived, many stepwells were abandoned, and some became rubbish dumps. Yet the pattern of their decline is revealing. The wells that survive in good condition are generally those that still serve a purpose for the neighbourhood, whether as a shrine, a tourist stop or a place where children play. Conservationists therefore argue that preserving a stepwell is as much a matter of restoring its social function as of repairing its stones. A restored monument that nobody visits, they warn, will slide towards neglect again within a generation. The lesson, in this view, extends beyond heritage: a structure that is woven into daily habits tends to be looked after, while one that is merely admired from a distance is quietly forgotten, however fine its carving may be.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage about the stepwells that have survived in good condition?

options.A: They were built with finer carving than the wells that were abandoned
options.B: They are all located in places visited by large numbers of tourists
options.C: They were repaired by villagers who refused to use piped water
options.D: They have usually remained useful to the people who live near them

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says the surviving wells 'are generally those that still serve a purpose for the neighbourhood', so continued usefulness is the supported inference. Shortcut: look for the line where the survivors are described, then match the option to that exact claim. Trap (A): Out-of-scope: the passage never compares the quality of carving in surviving and abandoned wells. Trap (B): Extreme scope: tourism is only one of several uses mentioned, so 'all' overstates the claim. Trap (C): Reversal/Out-of-scope: the passage does not say villagers refused piped water; it says disuse followed its arrival.

questions.concept_tag: Author's purpose - slow reading
questions.question_text:
Passage: Speed has become the unspoken virtue of modern reading. We skim headlines, scroll through summaries and measure ourselves by how many pages we clear in an evening. Against this habit, some teachers now champion what they call slow reading: returning to a short text several times, pausing over a single sentence, and writing a few lines in response before moving on. Advocates do not claim that all reading should be slow; a timetable or a news bulletin is rightly scanned in seconds. Their claim is narrower. Certain kinds of writing, such as a poem, a philosophical argument or a carefully built story, hide their richest meanings in details that a quick glance cannot register: a repeated word, a sudden shift of tone, a silence where an explanation might have been expected. Readers who rush discover what a text says; readers who linger discover how it works. Critics respond that slow reading is a luxury for those with free afternoons, and that students already struggle to finish their syllabus. The advocates reply that the practice is not about reading less but about reading differently, and that an hour spent in close attention can teach more than a week of hurried browsing. They also point out that the habit is portable: once a student learns to notice small details in a poem, the same alertness helps in reading a contract, a laboratory report or an advertisement. In their view, the real danger of speed is not that it wastes time but that it trains the mind to be satisfied with the surface, and a mind trained in that way finds depth tiresome even when depth is what the occasion demands.

The author's main purpose in the passage is to

options.A: prove that fast reading should be abandoned in schools
options.B: describe the daily reading routine of a particular group of teachers
options.C: present the case for slow reading and the response to its critics
options.D: argue that students should read fewer books each year

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage explains slow reading, states what advocates claim, and gives their reply to critics; the purpose is therefore to present the case and its defence. Shortcut: check which option covers the whole passage, not just one part. Trap (A): Extreme scope: advocates themselves say not all reading should be slow. Trap (B): Out-of-scope: the passage describes an idea, not a routine of named people. Trap (D): Reversal: the advocates say the point is reading differently, not reading less.

questions.concept_tag: Vocabulary in context - urban heat
questions.question_text:
Passage: On a summer afternoon, a dense neighbourhood can feel several degrees hotter than the farmland just outside the city. This effect, often called the urban heat island, arises because concrete, brick and asphalt absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night, so that streets never fully cool down. Dark rooftops make matters worse, and the heat given off by air conditioners adds to the load: each unit cools one room by pushing warm air into the street. Trees offer a surprisingly effective remedy. Their canopies shade the ground, and their leaves release water vapour, which cools the air much as perspiration cools the body. A single large tree can lower the temperature beneath it noticeably, and a row of trees along a road can make walking tolerable in the hottest weeks. Planners therefore encourage street planting, but the work is harder than it sounds. Young trees need water for years before they offer real shade, many pavements have too little soil for roots, and a tree planted without care often dies within a season. Some cities now pair tree planting with lighter-coloured roofs and paving, a combination that has reduced afternoon temperatures in trial districts. The measures are modest, none of them dramatic. But taken together they show that the heat of a city is not a fixed fact of life; it is partly the result of choices about materials and space, and choices can be changed.
