Residents who live in the hottest districts are often those with the fewest trees, and for them the remedy is not a luxury but a matter of health and daily comfort.

The word 'tolerable' in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Make walking tolerable in the hottest weeks' means walking becomes possible to endure, which is 'bearable'. Shortcut: substitute each option into the sentence and keep the one that preserves the sense. Trap (A): Extreme scope: the trees make walking bearable, not necessarily pleasant. Trap (C): Reversal: the sentence says the trees make the weather easier to endure. Trap (D): Reversal: 'tolerable' signals relief from hardship, not risk.

questions.concept_tag: Tone - translation and untranslatable words
questions.question_text:
Passage: Every translator learns early that a word is not a label stuck on an object but a small bundle of memories, habits and assumptions. When a Hindi speaker says 'ghar', the word carries more than a building with a roof; it includes the people who live there, the sounds of its mornings, the sense of belonging that makes a place a home. English has the word 'house' for the first meaning and 'home' for the second, but many languages have no such pair, and translators are left to decide which shade to keep. They are often accused of betrayal, as the old Italian pun puts it, yet the accusation misses what is truly difficult. A translator who stays too close to the original produces sentences that sound foreign and stiff; one who moves too far produces smooth prose that has quietly changed the author's meaning. A phrase that is playful in one language can sound rude in another, and a proverb that is warm in its own setting can sound merely odd when carried across without care. Good translations succeed by a series of small compromises, each defensible, none perfect. Readers rarely notice these compromises, and perhaps they should not; a translation that draws attention to itself has already failed in part. Still, it is worth remembering, when we praise a foreign novel for its 'beautiful prose', that we are praising the work of two writers, one of whom has stayed almost invisible. The translator deserves a more public share of the credit, since the choices made in a sentence can decide whether a distant author sounds alive or merely correct.

The tone of the author towards translators can best be described as
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author explains the difficulty of the work and ends by saying translators deserve more credit, so the tone is sympathetic and appreciative. Shortcut: read the concluding sentences; they usually reveal the author's attitude. Trap (A): Reversal: the author defends translators against the charge of betrayal. Trap (B): Out-of-scope: the closing call for credit shows clear sympathy. Trap (C): Out-of-scope: the pun is mentioned but the tone is serious and respectful.

questions.concept_tag: Inference - narrative of a sewing machine
questions.question_text:
Passage: After her husband died, Kamala did not sell the old sewing machine that stood in the corner of the front room. It was a heavy black thing with gold lettering rubbed almost invisible by decades of palms, and her son, now living in a city flat, had twice suggested that it be replaced by a modern one or simply given away. She smiled each time and changed the subject. On winter evenings she still oiled its wheel, though the neighbourhood tailor was cheaper and faster, and the click of the needle filled the room like a clock that had learned to speak. People in the lane brought her blouses to be mended, and she took only what they offered, sometimes a handful of vegetables or a cup of tea. When her granddaughter visited in the holidays, Kamala sat her at the machine and guided her hands, saying very little. The girl, impatient at first, found that the rhythm calmed her. On the last evening she asked her grandmother why she kept the machine when it was so old. Kamala looked at the faded letters and said that a machine was not old as long as someone still needed it to work. The girl did not fully understand, but she remembered the sentence all the way home on the train. Months later, when her own mother complained of a torn curtain, she found herself reaching for a needle, and realised with surprise that her hands already knew the beginning of the movement, which she had not been taught so much as given, quietly, one evening in a lamplit room.

Which of the following best captures the significance of the sewing machine for Kamala?

options.A: It links her to her past and to the usefulness she still finds in her work
options.B: It is a valuable antique that she hopes to sell at a good price
options.C: It is a burden that she keeps only because her son insists
options.D: It is the only way she can earn a living in the neighbourhood

questions.pedagogical_explanation: She will not sell or replace it, keeps it working and teaches her granddaughter on it, so it connects her past with a sense of continuing usefulness. Shortcut: track her actions, not just the narrator's description. Trap (B): Reversal: she refuses to sell or give it away. Trap (C): Reversal: it is the son who wants it replaced, and she resists. Trap (D): Extreme scope: she takes only small gifts, so it is not her only income.

questions.concept_tag: Main idea - the living soil
questions.question_text:
Passage: To most people, soil is simply the brown stuff under their feet, the inert ground in which plants happen to stand. Farmers and scientists know better. A handful of healthy soil can contain more living organisms than there are people in a large city: bacteria, fungi, worms, tiny insects and threads of root that together make up a community of extraordinary complexity. These organisms break down fallen leaves and dead roots into nutrients that plants can absorb, bind soil particles together so that rain does not wash them away, and store water through dry weeks. Fungal threads, in particular, form networks that exchange nutrients with plant roots in return for sugars. When soil is ploughed too often, drenched with chemicals or left bare between harvests, this community suffers, and the land slowly loses its fertility even if it still looks like good earth. Recovery is possible but slow. Farmers who keep a cover of plants through the year, add compost and disturb the ground less often report that their fields hold moisture better and need fewer inputs within a few seasons. None of this is dramatic enough to make headlines, and that is part of the difficulty: the damage is gradual, the benefits of care are gradual, and neither is easy to see from the road. Yet a nation's food supply rests upon the quiet working of this hidden community. To treat soil as a dead substance is to misunderstand what we depend on, and a misunderstanding of this kind has consequences that arrive slowly and are hard to undo.

The central idea of the passage is that

options.A: chemical fertilisers are the main cause of damage to soil
options.B: worms and insects matter more than fungi for plant growth
options.C: farmers should stop ploughing their fields altogether
options.D: soil is a living system whose health underlies agriculture and deserves careful treatment

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage describes soil as a community of organisms, explains how it is damaged and restored, and warns about misunderstanding it; the central idea is that soil is living and needs care. Shortcut: the main idea must cover the whole passage, so reject options built on a single detail. Trap (A): Extreme scope: chemicals are one of several causes mentioned, not the main cause. Trap (B): Out-of-scope: the passage does not rank these organisms against one another. Trap (C): Extreme scope: the passage says ploughing too often harms soil, not that it should stop.

questions.concept_tag: Inference - assessment debate
questions.question_text:
Passage: The debate over examinations is old, but it has lately become sharper. Supporters of a single, final test argue that it is fair in a plain sense: every student answers the same questions under the same conditions, and the marks can be compared without suspicion. Continuous assessment, they say, depends on teachers' judgement, and judgement can be swayed by liking, by prejudice or by pressure from parents. Opponents reply that a single test measures a narrow range of skills, rewards memory and exam technique, and puts too much weight on a performance that may be spoiled by illness or nerves on a given morning. A student who has worked steadily for two years can lose everything in three hours. Teachers who have watched a capable student freeze in the hall know how costly such a morning can be. A fair system, they argue, should record progress over time, using projects, class tests and practical work. Each side is partly right, and the better schemes try to borrow from both. Some countries combine a school-based record with a moderated external test, and train teachers to mark against shared standards so that judgement is less personal. The combination is more expensive and more demanding than either extreme, and it requires trust in teachers that some systems are reluctant to give. Even so, it has the merit of treating a student as a person who develops over years rather than as a candidate who performs for an afternoon. The question is therefore not which method is perfect, since none is, but how to reduce the weaknesses of each while keeping its strengths.

Which of the following statements would the author most likely agree with?

options.A: A single final test is unfair because every student answers the same questions
options.B: Teachers' judgement should be removed from assessment altogether
options.C: A system that blends school records with a moderated test can reduce the weaknesses of both methods
options.D: Continuous assessment is cheaper and easier to run than a final test

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author concludes that neither extreme is perfect and that blended schemes reduce the weaknesses of each; only the blended-system option matches this. Shortcut: identify the author's own conclusion, usually in the last few lines. Trap (A): Reversal: sameness of questions is described as the test's chief claim to fairness. Trap (B): Extreme scope: the author supports training teachers, not removing their judgement. Trap (D): Reversal: the passage says the blended approach is more expensive and demanding.

questions.concept_tag: Logical inference - Silk Route exchange
questions.question_text:
Passage: The Silk Route was never a single road. It was a shifting network of tracks linking oases, river valleys and mountain passes, along which merchants carried silk, spices, glass, paper and horses over distances no single trader could cover. Goods usually changed hands many times: a bolt of silk might pass through a dozen merchants before reaching a buyer in the west, each adding a margin to its price. Caravan leaders hired guides, guards and interpreters at each stage, and the costs of these services were passed along the chain. Yet what travelled with the caravans was not only merchandise. Monks carried scriptures and styles of painting across deserts, craftsmen learned techniques from foreign colleagues, and common words slipped from language to language in the markets where traders bargained. The spread of papermaking westwards, for instance, changed how knowledge was recorded and shared, and no merchant had planned it. Historians stress that the route was also a fragile one. Political upheaval, banditry or a change in climate could close a pass for years, and cities that had grown rich on the trade could decline quickly once the caravans turned elsewhere. Several oasis towns that once held thousands of residents are now little more than ruins in the sand. The Silk Route therefore teaches two lessons at once: that contact between distant societies can transform them in ways nobody intends, and that prosperity built on a single channel of trade is easily lost. Such lessons are not confined to the past, for any modern economy that depends on one supply line or one buyer faces a similar risk, whatever its apparent wealth.

Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the passage?

options.A: Merchants deliberately planned the spread of papermaking to the west
options.B: Exchange along the route spread ideas as well as goods, and the towns that depended on it were vulnerable
options.C: The Silk Route was a single, well-maintained highway controlled by one power
options.D: Only silk was valuable enough to be traded over long distances

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The two lessons stated in the passage are that contact spreads unintended influences and that dependence on one channel is risky; only the first option reflects both. Shortcut: match each option against the specific statements of the passage. Trap (A): Reversal: the passage says no merchant had planned it. Trap (C): Reversal: the passage calls it a shifting network, not a single road. Trap (D): Extreme scope: the passage lists many goods, including spices, glass and horses.

questions.concept_tag: Author's attitude - folk theatre
questions.question_text:
Passage: Few traditional art forms have been as resilient as the folk theatre of northern India. In the village square, under a hanging lamp, a troupe of men and boys would perform for hours, shifting between song, dialogue and dance, with a drummer driving the action and a clown puncturing solemn moments. The stories were drawn from legend and local history, but they were rarely told straight. A comic servant would make fun of the king, and the audience, which knew the story by heart, enjoyed the jokes more than the plot. Such theatre could comment on landlords, officials and even village scandals with an ease that other forms did not allow, because everything that was said could be passed off as part of the play. When cinema arrived, many predicted the end of these troupes, and certainly the audiences shrank. Yet some troupes adapted, borrowing film songs, shortening performances and appearing at fairs and weddings. Others disappeared, and with them went the knowledge of how to sing particular tunes or paint particular masks. Travelling companies often rehearsed in courtyards for weeks, and a single family might preserve the same role for several generations. It would be easy to romanticise this world, and the author does not wish to do so: performers were often poor, and the art depended on patrons who set their own limits on what could be said. But it would be equally unwise to dismiss it as a relic. It was, and in places still is, a living way for ordinary people to laugh at power and tell their own stories in their own idiom.

The author's attitude to folk theatre is best described as

options.A: balanced, admiring its vitality without romanticising its conditions
options.B: nostalgic, longing for a golden age that has vanished
options.C: dismissive, regarding it as a relic of little value
options.D: indifferent, merely recording facts about the performances

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author praises the living quality of the form and also notes poverty and patrons' limits, so the attitude is balanced and admiring but not romantic. Shortcut: look for words that signal appreciation and reservation together. Trap (B): Reversal: the author explicitly refuses to romanticise the past. Trap (C): Reversal: the author calls it unwise to dismiss it as a relic. Trap (D): Out-of-scope: the author clearly expresses appreciation and caution.

questions.concept_tag: Inference - procrastination and emotion
questions.question_text:
Passage: Procrastination is usually described as a failure of time management, and so the advice given to those who suffer from it is to make lists, set alarms and break large jobs into small steps. These tips help some people, but psychologists who study delay have noticed that they often miss the point. When a student puts off writing an essay, the problem is rarely that he cannot find the hour. It is that the essay arouses an unpleasant feeling, such as boredom, anxiety or a fear of doing badly, and avoiding the task gives immediate relief from that feeling. The relief is a reward, and rewards strengthen habits. In this view, procrastination is a way of managing mood in the short term at the cost of one's interests in the long term. The theory explains why people delay even tasks that are quite simple, and why guilt about delay does not cure it: guilt is itself an unpleasant feeling that the person is tempted to avoid by turning to something more comfortable. Researchers therefore suggest methods that deal with feelings directly. One is to begin with a very small portion of the work, such as five minutes, so that the dread of the whole task loosens its hold. Another is to treat oneself with kindness after a lapse instead of with harsh blame, since students who forgive themselves are found more likely to return to the work than those who punish themselves. The remedy, in short, begins with understanding what delay does for the person delaying.

According to the passage, why does guilt fail to cure procrastination?

options.A: Guilt is itself unpleasant, so the person is tempted to avoid it by turning to something more comfortable
options.B: Guilt makes the person forget the deadline for the task
options.C: People who feel guilty always have poor time-management skills
options.D: Guilt rewards the person with relief from the unpleasant task

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says guilt is 'itself an unpleasant feeling that the person is tempted to avoid', which keeps the cycle going. Shortcut: find the sentence that follows 'guilt' and restate it in your own words. Trap (B): Out-of-scope: the passage never says guilt causes forgetfulness. Trap (C): Extreme scope: the passage argues that time management is not the real problem. Trap (D): Half-true: avoidance, not guilt, gives relief; guilt adds another feeling to escape.

questions.concept_tag: Inference - night train journey
questions.question_text:
Passage: The night train left the station twenty minutes late, and Ishaan, who had boarded it in a mood of quiet resentment, found his berth already occupied by a stranger's luggage. He had not wanted to make this journey. His father had insisted that he attend the wedding of a cousin he barely knew, and he had packed in silence, fully intending to leave the next afternoon. His mother had slipped a small packet of sweets into his bag, which he found only when the train was already moving. As the train gathered speed, the compartment settled into a murmur of unpacking, and an elderly man across the aisle offered him a share of a packet of roasted peanuts without asking his name. Ishaan accepted, rather stiffly. Through the window the lights of small towns slid by and vanished, and the old man began to speak, not to him in particular, but to the dark: about a village where he had taught for thirty years, about former pupils who now sent him letters from distant cities. Ishaan listened despite himself. Somewhere past midnight, he realised that his irritation had loosened its hold, and that he was curious about the cousin, the wedding and the unknown relatives waiting at the other end. He did not say so, and the old man did not seem to expect it. When the train finally slowed into the grey light of a small platform, Ishaan found that he was the first at the door, bag in hand, looking out for faces he could not yet name, with a readiness that would have surprised him the evening before.

Which of the following best describes the change in Ishaan during the journey?

options.A: He moves from curiosity to resentment
options.B: He moves from reluctance to curiosity and readiness
options.C: He remains resentful but hides it politely
options.D: He decides to return home the next afternoon

questions.pedagogical_explanation: He begins resentful and silent, listens to the old man, becomes curious about the wedding and arrives eager to meet people, so the shift is from reluctance to curiosity and readiness. Shortcut: trace the character's feelings at the beginning, middle and end. Trap (A): Reversal: the passage shows resentment giving way to curiosity. Trap (C): Reversal: his irritation 'loosened its hold'. Trap (D): Reversal: he intended to leave at first, but by the end he is eager to arrive.

questions.concept_tag: Inference - lighthouse automation
questions.question_text:
Passage: For more than two centuries, the lighthouse keeper was a familiar figure on rocky coasts: a person who trimmed wicks, polished lenses, wound clockwork and watched the sea through storms. Many stations stood on rocks so exposed that supplies could be landed only in calm weather, and families waited weeks for letters. The work was lonely and dangerous, and the keepers' logbooks, which survive in large numbers, record the weather with a patient precision that historians now use to study past climate. Automation changed all this. Electric lamps replaced oil flames, sensors began to switch lights on at dusk, and remote monitoring made it possible for one technician on land to supervise dozens of stations. The change brought undeniable benefits: it saved money, removed human beings from remote and risky posts, and made the lights more reliable. But it also removed something less easy to measure. A keeper noticed when a fishing boat did not return, when a ship drifted too close to rocks or when a distant flare signalled trouble, and responded on the spot. A sensor can report a failed bulb but not a flare. Some coastal communities have therefore asked for volunteers to keep a regular watch at disused stations, not to run the light but to keep a pair of eyes on the water. The episode shows a general pattern in technological change: a task is broken into its measurable parts, the parts are automated, and a hidden part of the work, one nobody thought to write down, quietly disappears with the worker who did it.

Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.A: The Dangers of Life on a Rocky Coast
options.B: Why Electric Lamps Are Better Than Oil Flames
options.C: What Automation Took Away from the Lighthouse
options.D: The Weather Records of Lighthouse Keepers

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage moves from the keeper's role to automation and ends on the hidden loss, so the title must reflect what automation removed. Shortcut: a good title covers the passage's full argument, including its conclusion. Trap (A): Out-of-scope: danger is mentioned but is not the theme. Trap (B): Extreme scope: the passage notes benefits but its point is what was lost. Trap (D): Out-of-scope: the logbooks are a supporting detail, not the main idea.

questions.concept_tag: Assumption - public libraries and democracy
questions.question_text:
Passage: A public library is one of the few institutions in which a person may spend an entire day without being asked to buy anything. That simple fact explains much of its value. In a library, a retired clerk, a schoolgirl preparing for an examination and a job seeker updating a résumé share the same tables and draw on the same shelves, and none of them needs to prove that they deserve to be there. Staff at the desk rarely ask why a reader wants a particular book, and they treat a question about a dictionary with the same seriousness as one about a thesis. Defenders of public libraries argue that this mixing is democratic in a deeper sense than voting: it gives every citizen access to the information on which sound judgement depends. They also observe that libraries now serve purposes that their founders never imagined, such as offering internet access to those who lack it, running classes for new readers and providing quiet places to study to those whose homes are crowded. Sceptics reply that in an age of online search, a building full of books is an expensive habit. The defenders respond that the sceptics assume that everyone can afford a device and a connection, and that a search engine can replace the skill of a librarian who helps a reader frame a question. Whatever the answer, the argument shows that a library should be judged not by the number of books it lends but by the number of people it quietly equips to make their own decisions, and that this kind of value is rarely captured by figures in an annual report.

The defenders' reply to the sceptics rests on the assumption that

options.A: not everyone has the means to use online search on their own
options.B: books are more reliable than online information
options.C: libraries earn enough money to pay for themselves
options.D: every citizen already has a device and a connection

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The defenders say the sceptics 'assume that everyone can afford a device and a connection'; their own reply therefore assumes the opposite, that not everyone can. Shortcut: an assumption is what must be true for the argument to work; ask what the reply takes for granted. Trap (B): Out-of-scope: reliability of sources is not discussed. Trap (C): Out-of-scope: finances of libraries are not discussed. Trap (D): Reversal: the defenders say the sceptics assume this, and they reject it.

questions.concept_tag: Inference - science communication and uncertainty
questions.question_text:
Passage: When scientists speak to the public, they face a dilemma that their training has not prepared them for. In their own journals, caution is a virtue: a finding is reported with its margin of error, the limits of the sample and the alternative explanations that remain open. In a news bulletin, the same caution can sound like evasion. A researcher who says that a medicine 'probably' helps most patients may be heard as saying that nobody knows whether it works. Some respond by dropping their qualifications and speaking with a confidence they do not feel; when later evidence forces a revision, the public concludes that scientists keep changing their minds, and trust suffers. Others hide behind a wall of technical language that no listener can follow. A few simply decline interviews, and the gap they leave is filled by people with less knowledge and more confidence. A better course, communicators suggest, is to be open about the shape of uncertainty without being paralysed by it: to say what is well established, what is likely and what is still unknown, and to explain that revision is how the method works, not a sign that it has failed. Citizens who are told early that knowledge grows by correction are better prepared when correction comes. It is not an easy skill, and it is rarely rewarded in a scientist's career, where publications count for more than public explanation. But the cost of neglecting it is real: a public that has learned to distrust uncertainty is easily persuaded by anyone who offers certainty, even when that certainty has nothing behind it.

According to the passage, which approach to public communication do the communicators recommend?

options.A: Dropping all qualifications so that statements sound confident
options.B: Using technical language to protect the precision of a finding
options.C: Avoiding public statements until a result is certain
options.D: Explaining what is established, what is likely and what is unknown, and why revision is normal

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage recommends being open about the shape of uncertainty: established, likely and unknown, and presenting revision as part of the method. Shortcut: find the sentence introducing 'a better course' and paraphrase it. Trap (A): Reversal: this is described as a mistaken response that damages trust. Trap (B): Reversal: technical walls are criticised because no listener can follow them. Trap (C): Out-of-scope: the passage never recommends silence.

questions.concept_tag: Inference - handloom revival
questions.question_text:
Passage: Handloom weaving in India has long been celebrated as a symbol of heritage and skill, yet the weavers themselves have seldom benefited from the praise. A weaver's day often begins before dawn, and a single length of cloth can take a week to finish, which makes its price in the market seem small. Their cloth competes with machine-made fabric that is cheaper and produced in vast quantities, and many families have given up the loom for work in construction or factories. Recent attempts at revival have therefore concentrated on a shift in how the cloth is sold rather than how it is made. Cooperative societies now help weavers to buy yarn in bulk, reach customers in distant cities through online catalogues and receive a larger share of the final price. Designers, too, have begun to work with weavers, adapting traditional patterns to the clothes people actually wear. Early results are encouraging, though uneven. In places where the cooperative is well run and the designer treats the weaver as a partner, incomes have risen and young people have started to return. In places where the project is a brief fashion enterprise, the weavers often find that orders disappear when the season changes, leaving them with debts for yarn they cannot repay. Observers conclude that revival depends less on public enthusiasm than on structure: fair prices, steady orders and a say in design. Admiration for a craft does not feed a family; a market that pays properly and persistently does, and an industry that holds a heritage in trust should therefore measure its success by what happens in the weaver's household rather than by the applause in the city's showrooms.

Which of the following is supported by the passage?

options.A: Revival has failed everywhere because machine-made cloth is cheaper
options.B: Weavers prefer factory work to weaving whenever it is available
options.C: Revival succeeds where weavers receive fair prices, steady orders and a voice in design
options.D: Public enthusiasm alone is enough to sustain the craft

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage concludes that revival depends on fair prices, steady orders and a say in design, so the first option is supported. Shortcut: avoid options that use words such as 'everywhere' or 'always' unless the passage does. Trap (A): Extreme scope: results are described as encouraging though uneven. Trap (B): Out-of-scope: the passage says some families have left, not that all prefer to. Trap (D): Reversal: the passage says revival depends less on enthusiasm than on structure.

questions.concept_tag: Inference - limits of monsoon forecasting
questions.question_text:
Passage: Each year, millions of farmers wait for the forecast of the monsoon, and each year the forecast seems to be both useful and disappointing. Newspapers print the figures on their front pages, and conversations in tea shops turn to the clouds long before the first drops fall. It is useful because it gives a general picture: whether the season as a whole is likely to bring rain above or below the long-term average. It disappoints because farmers need to know something more local, such as whether rain will fall on their district in the third week of June, and no forecast made months in advance can say so. The reason lies in the nature of the atmosphere, in which small differences in conditions grow quickly, so that predictions become less reliable the further ahead they look. Scientists have improved the models, the satellites and the computing power available to them, and short-range forecasts of a few days are now far better than they were a generation ago. Seasonal forecasts have gained less, because the large patterns that guide the monsoon, such as ocean temperatures, can be measured but do not fix the pattern of individual storms. Experts therefore advise farmers to treat the seasonal forecast as a guide to planning, not as a promise, and to combine it with the short-range alerts that are now widely sent to mobile phones. Treated in this way, the forecast supports good decisions; treated as a prophecy, it merely produces anger when the weather refuses to oblige. The sensible attitude is to ask not whether a forecast was right but whether it helped one choose well.

Why do seasonal forecasts disappoint farmers, according to the passage?

options.A: Satellites and computing power have not improved at all
options.B: They cannot tell farmers when and where rain will fall in a given district
options.C: Ocean temperatures cannot be measured accurately
options.D: Short-range forecasts are less reliable than they used to be

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says farmers need local detail that a forecast made months in advance cannot give; every other option contradicts a stated fact. Shortcut: underline the reason clause after 'because' in the passage. Trap (A): Reversal: the passage says these have improved. Trap (C): Reversal: the passage says they can be measured but do not fix individual storms. Trap (D): Reversal: short-range forecasts are described as far better than before.

questions.concept_tag: Inference - the exam hall
questions.question_text:
Passage: The invigilator had barely finished reading the instructions when Nandini noticed that her hand was trembling. She looked down at the paper, face-down on the desk, and felt an old, familiar panic that no amount of revision had managed to dispel. The clock above the blackboard ticked loudly, and a fan turned slowly overhead without moving much air. Around her, other candidates adjusted pens and rulers with a calm that seemed unfair. She remembered her teacher's advice, given in the corridor that morning, to read the entire paper first and begin with whatever felt easiest, and when the signal was given she turned the page with the slow care of someone defusing a device. The first question was not easy, and neither was the second. The third, however, was about a poem she had once copied out for no reason except that she liked it, and she found, to her astonishment, that she could say exactly what she wanted. By the time she reached the fifth question, her handwriting had steadied, and she realised that the trembling had stopped without her noticing the moment. She did not finish the paper in the end; two questions remained, and the bell sounded while she was still writing the last line of the previous answer. Walking out, she was surprised to find that she did not feel defeated. She felt, instead, like someone who had visited a frightening place and discovered that it had ordinary corridors and exits, and that she had walked through it on her own two feet.

What does the ending of the passage suggest about Nandini?

options.A: She is certain that she has performed better than anyone else
options.B: She has gained confidence from facing her fear even though the outcome is incomplete
options.C: She regrets having chosen to answer the third question first
options.D: She feels defeated because she did not finish the paper

questions.pedagogical_explanation: She did not finish, yet feels like someone who has crossed a frightening place on her own feet, which suggests increased confidence. Shortcut: read the final lines for the character's emotional state. Trap (A): Extreme scope: nothing suggests she compares herself with others. Trap (C): Out-of-scope: the third question helped her; regret is not mentioned. Trap (D): Reversal: the passage says she did not feel defeated.

questions.concept_tag: Inference - maps as arguments
questions.question_text:
Passage: A map seems to be a neutral picture of the world, but every map is an argument about what matters. A cartographer must decide what to include and what to leave out, which names to print in large type, where to draw borders and how to flatten a curved surface onto a flat sheet. Each decision, however small, carries an assumption. Even the choice of colour, which seems purely decorative, tells the reader what to notice first and what to ignore. The familiar world map used in many classrooms, for example, enlarges regions near the poles so that countries in the north look far larger than they are, and for centuries this quietly suggested a world in which Europe and North America filled the stage. A different projection can reverse that impression, but at the cost of distorting other features, since no flat map can be accurate in every respect. Maps made by governments often reveal their purposes in what they omit: a disputed boundary may be drawn as settled, a village may vanish from the page because it does not appear in the official records. Communities have therefore begun to draw their own maps, marking forests they depend on, paths their children walk to school, and sites that are sacred to them. Such maps are not more truthful than the official ones, but they show who has been left out. A reader who knows that a map is an argument will ask who drew it, for whom and with what purpose, and will therefore see more in it than the neat lines convey.

The author's main point about maps is that

options.A: maps made by communities are more accurate than government maps
options.B: flat maps should be replaced by globes in all schools
options.C: governments always draw maps that hide the truth
options.D: every map reflects choices and so should be read critically

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The opening sentence and the last lines show that maps carry decisions and should be read by asking who drew them and why. Shortcut: the first and last sentences often state the thesis. Trap (A): Reversal: the passage says community maps are not more truthful, only revealing. Trap (B): Out-of-scope: the passage does not suggest replacing flat maps. Trap (C): Extreme scope: 'always' overstates a point made about some maps.

questions.concept_tag: Inference - tools shape thought
questions.question_text:
Passage: Writers have always been uneasy about the tools of their trade, and each new device has been accused of damaging thought. Ancient teachers feared that writing itself would weaken memory; later critics said the same of print, and then of the typewriter. Their fears were partly justified, though not in the way they imagined. Memory did not vanish, but it was redirected: people who could consult a page no longer needed to carry an entire epic in their heads, and the training that once made such feats possible faded. Each time, the old habits were defended as the proper discipline of the mind, and the new devices were treated with suspicion. The typewriter changed style in subtler ways. A writer who once composed slowly in ink, crossing out and rewriting, found that clean pages encouraged rapid drafts and early revision, and some complained that their sentences had become more mechanical. The computer's keyboard has taken this process further, since text can now be rearranged without a trace. Yet it would be wrong to conclude that a tool simply makes the writer better or worse. What it does is alter the habits of composition, and these habits in turn shape what is easy to think and what is hard. A writer who knows this can choose, at times, to write by hand in order to slow down, or to use the screen in order to speed up. The question to ask of any new tool is therefore not whether it is good or bad but what it makes easy, what it makes difficult and whether one is content with that change.

The passage suggests that a writing tool

options.A: changes the habits of composition and thereby influences how easily certain thoughts are formed
options.B: always makes the writer more skilled than before
options.C: has no effect on the quality of a writer's thinking
options.D: is accepted by writers without any concern

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author says a tool alters the habits of composition and so shapes what is easy or hard to think; this matches the first option. Shortcut: eliminate options that use absolutes such as 'always' or 'no effect'. Trap (B): Extreme scope: the passage says a tool does not simply make the writer better. Trap (C): Reversal: the passage says tools alter habits that shape thought. Trap (D): Reversal: the opening says writers have always been uneasy about tools.

questions.concept_tag: Inference - birdsong dialects
questions.question_text:
Passage: Many people assume that a bird sings the same song throughout its species, as though the tune were stored in its body like the colour of its feathers. In truth, the songs of many birds are learned, and they vary from place to place in ways that resemble human dialects. A young bird listens to adult males near its nest, memorises their phrases and practises them for weeks before it can produce a full song. If it is raised in isolation, it sings a rough and unformed version that other birds respond to poorly. Researchers who compared populations of the same species living in different valleys found regular differences in the order and pitch of their notes, and birds sometimes responded more strongly to the local song than to a recording from a distant region. Such differences are heard most clearly in species that live in separate valleys or on separate islands. The pattern has consequences. A population whose song drifts far from the neighbouring one may find that its members no longer recognise each other as mates, and over long periods this can contribute to the formation of separate species. Cities have added a new twist: in noisy streets, some birds sing at higher pitch or louder volume so that their voices are not drowned out by traffic. Whether such changes will become permanent is not yet known. But they remind us that behaviour, even in creatures with tiny brains, can be passed on by learning and can change within a few generations when the surroundings change.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: All birds learn their songs from adult males of other species
options.B: Birds raised in isolation sing more beautifully than other birds
options.C: Learning allows bird songs to change when the environment changes
options.D: Noisy cities have permanently changed the songs of all urban birds

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Songs are learned, differ by place, and shift in noisy cities, so learning allows change with surroundings. Shortcut: avoid answers that turn 'some' into 'all' or 'not yet known' into 'permanent'. Trap (A): Extreme scope: the passage speaks of many birds and adult males near the nest. Trap (B): Reversal: isolated birds sing a rough and unformed version. Trap (D): Extreme scope: it is not yet known whether the changes will be permanent, and not all birds are mentioned.

questions.concept_tag: Subject-verb agreement - collective subject
questions.question_text: Choose the correct option to fill in the blank: The team of players ___ arriving tomorrow.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Rule: the verb agrees with the head noun, not the noun nearest to it. The head noun is 'team' (singular), so the verb is 'is'. Shortcut: ignore the phrase starting with 'of' and find the head noun. Trap (A): Plural verb: the subject is 'team', which is singular, not 'players'. Trap (B): Wrong tense: 'tomorrow' needs a present or future form, not a past form. Trap (D): Wrong form: 'arriving' needs the helping verb 'is' or 'are' (present continuous).

questions.concept_tag: Articles - a before a vowel sound
questions.question_text: Choose the correct article: She is ___ honest girl.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Rule: use 'an' before a vowel sound, not just a vowel letter. 'Honest' begins with the sound /o/, so 'an honest girl'. Shortcut: say the word aloud; the first sound decides. Trap (B): Wrong: 'honest' starts with a vowel sound (the h is silent), so 'a' is wrong. Trap (C): Wrong: no particular girl is being identified, so the definite article does not fit. Trap (D): Wrong: a singular countable noun phrase needs an article here.

questions.concept_tag: Prepositions - adjective with preposition
questions.question_text: Choose the correct preposition: He is very good ___ mathematics.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Rule: 'good at' is used for a skill or subject. So, 'good at mathematics'. Shortcut: learn adjective-preposition pairs as phrases. Trap (B): Wrong: 'good in' is not the standard collocation for a skill. Trap (C): Wrong: 'on' shows contact or topic, not skill. Trap (D): Wrong: 'good for' means beneficial, as in 'good for health'.

questions.concept_tag: Synonyms - brave
questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to BRAVE.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Brave means ready to face danger or pain; 'courageous' has the same sense. Shortcut: match the meaning, not the first letter. Trap (A): Different meaning: careful means cautious, not fearless. Trap (C): Different meaning: clever refers to intelligence. Trap (D): Different meaning: cheerful refers to a happy mood.

questions.concept_tag: Tenses - simple present for habits
questions.question_text: Choose the correct form: She ___ to school every day.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Every day' signals a habit, so use the simple present. With 'she' (third person singular) add -es to 'go': 'goes'. Shortcut: habit words such as 'every day' call for the simple present. Trap (A): Wrong: a third-person singular subject needs 'goes'. Trap (B): Wrong: 'going' alone is not a finite verb. Trap (D): Wrong: 'gone' is a past participle and needs a helping verb.

questions.concept_tag: Plurals - irregular nouns
questions.question_text: Choose the correct plural of 'child'.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Child' has an irregular plural, 'children', formed with -ren. Shortcut: learn the common irregular plurals: men, women, children, feet, teeth. Trap (A): Wrong: 'child' does not take a plain -s. Trap (C): Wrong: no such plural exists. Trap (D): Wrong: 'children' is already plural; -s makes it incorrect.

questions.concept_tag: Spelling - commonly misspelt word
questions.question_text: Choose the correctly spelt word.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The correct spelling is 'necessary': one c, double s, ending -ary. Shortcut: remember: one collar (c) and two sleeves (ss). Trap (A): Wrong: it doubles the c; the correct spelling has a single c followed by e. Trap (B): Wrong: it needs a double s. Trap (C): Wrong: the ending is -ary, not -ery.

questions.concept_tag: One-word substitution - author
questions.question_text: Choose the one word for 'a person who writes books'.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The person who writes books is an author. Shortcut: identify the action in the phrase: writes. Trap (A): Different role: an editor corrects and prepares a text for publication. Trap (B): Different role: a publisher prints and sells books. Trap (C): Different role: a reader reads books.

questions.concept_tag: Idioms - under the weather
questions.question_text: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'under the weather'.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The idiom 'under the weather' means feeling slightly ill or low in spirits. Shortcut: idioms are decided by usage, not by the words. Trap (A): Literal reading: the idiom is not about weather conditions. Trap (C): Reversal: the idiom suggests poor health, not happiness. Trap (D): Unrelated: the idiom has nothing to do with preparation.

questions.concept_tag: Pronouns - possessive adjectives
questions.question_text: Choose the correct option: Rina and I finished ___ work early.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Rina and I' means 'we', so the possessive form is 'our'. Shortcut: replace the subject with a single pronoun (we) and then take its possessive. Trap (A): Wrong: the subject is 'Rina and I', which is plural, so 'my' is wrong. Trap (B): Wrong: 'their' refers to other people; the speaker is included. Trap (D): Wrong: 'her' leaves out the speaker.

questions.concept_tag: Conjunctions - contrast
questions.question_text: Choose the correct conjunction: He was tired, ___ he kept working.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The two clauses contrast: tired but still working. 'Yet' joins contrasting ideas. Shortcut: ask whether the second part agrees with or opposes the first. Trap (B): Wrong: 'so' shows result; tiredness does not lead to working. Trap (C): Wrong: 'because' gives a reason; tiredness is not a reason to keep working. Trap (D): Wrong: 'or' gives alternatives.

questions.concept_tag: Voice - active to passive reversal
questions.question_text: Choose the correct active form of: 'The letter was written by Mohan.'
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In the active voice, the doer becomes the subject: 'Mohan'. 'Was written' becomes 'wrote'. Shortcut: keep the tense the same when changing voice. Trap (A): Wrong tense: the passive uses 'was written' (past), so the active must be past. Trap (C): Wrong tense: present perfect does not match the simple past. Trap (D): Wrong sense: the letter did not do the writing.

questions.concept_tag: Narration - direct to indirect
questions.question_text: Choose the correct indirect speech: He said, "I am happy."

options.A: He said that I am happy.
options.B: He said that he is happy.
options.C: He said that he had been happy.
options.D: He said that he was happy.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Rule: with a past reporting verb, present tense changes to past tense and the pronoun changes to match the speaker. 'I am' becomes 'he was'. Shortcut: backshift one step: present to past. Trap (A): Wrong: the pronoun 'I' should become 'he' and the tense should shift. Trap (B): Wrong: after the reporting verb 'said' (past), the present tense 'am' changes to 'was'. Trap (C): Wrong: a simple present changes to a simple past, not past perfect.

questions.concept_tag: Sentence correction - agreement with 'does'
questions.question_text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: With a singular third-person subject the helping verb is 'does'. After 'does' or 'doesn't', use the base form 'like'. Shortcut: the helping verb carries the -s; the main verb stays plain. Trap (A): Wrong: 'don't' does not agree with the singular subject 'she'. Trap (C): Wrong: after 'doesn't' the verb stays in its base form. Trap (D): Wrong: negation needs the helping verb 'does'.

questions.concept_tag: Homophones - bear and bare
questions.question_text: Choose the correct word to fill in the blank: I could not ___ the noise any longer.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Bear' here means to tolerate. 'Bare' means naked, which does not suit the sentence. Shortcut: check the meaning in the sentence, not the sound. Trap (A): Wrong: 'bare' means uncovered or empty. Trap (B): Wrong: 'beer' is a drink. Trap (D): Wrong: 'bier' is a stand for a coffin.

questions.concept_tag: Collective nouns - bees
questions.question_text: Choose the correct collective noun: A ___ of bees.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A group of bees is called a swarm. Shortcut: memorise the common collective nouns in pairs. Trap (B): Wrong: a herd is used for cattle and other animals. Trap (C): Wrong: a pack is used for wolves or dogs. Trap (D): Wrong: a flock is used for birds or sheep.

questions.concept_tag: Degrees of comparison - two-syllable and longer adjectives
questions.question_text: Choose the correct option: This book is ___ than that one.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Than' signals a comparison between two things. A long adjective such as 'interesting' forms its comparative with 'more'. Shortcut: 'than' needs a comparative form. Trap (A): Wrong: the superlative needs three or more items. Trap (B): Wrong: long adjectives take 'more', not -er. Trap (C): Wrong: double comparison is incorrect.

questions.concept_tag: Question tags - negative tag for positive statement
questions.question_text: Choose the correct question tag: You are coming, ___?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A positive statement takes a negative tag, built with the same helping verb: 'are' becomes 'aren't you'. Shortcut: repeat the helping verb and flip positive to negative. Trap (B): Wrong: a positive statement takes a negative tag. Trap (C): Wrong: the tag must repeat the helping verb 'are'. Trap (D): Wrong: 'isn't' does not agree with 'you'.

questions.concept_tag: Sentence correction - neither with a singular verb
questions.question_text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.

options.A: Neither of the candidates have submitted the form.
options.B: Neither of the candidates submit the form yesterday.
options.C: Neither of the candidates has submitted the form.
options.D: Neither candidates has submitted the form.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Rule: 'neither of' + plural noun takes a singular verb. So 'Neither of the candidates has submitted the form.' Shortcut: the subject word is 'neither', not 'candidates'. Trap (A): Wrong: 'neither' is singular, so it takes 'has', not 'have'. Trap (B): Wrong: the verb form clashes with the time word 'yesterday' and with the singular subject. Trap (D): Wrong: 'neither' must be followed by 'of the' before a plural noun.

questions.concept_tag: Conditionals - third conditional
questions.question_text: Choose the correct option: Had I known about the delay, I ___ earlier.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Had I known' is an inverted third conditional (if I had known). The result clause takes 'would have' + past participle: 'would have left'. Shortcut: 'had + subject' at the start signals the third conditional. Trap (A): Wrong: a past unreal condition cannot take a future result. Trap (B): Wrong: this refers to a present unreal situation, not a past one. Trap (C): Wrong: the result clause needs 'would have', not the past perfect.

questions.concept_tag: Synonyms - tenacious
questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to TENACIOUS.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Tenacious means holding firmly to a purpose, which is 'persistent'. Shortcut: tenacious = holds on and does not let go. Trap (B): Sound-alike meaning: temporary means lasting a short time. Trap (C): Sound-alike word: tender means gentle or soft. Trap (D): Different meaning: timid means lacking courage.

questions.concept_tag: Idioms - let the cat out of the bag
questions.question_text: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'to let the cat out of the bag'.

options.C: to reveal a secret by mistake

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The idiom means to disclose a secret, usually by accident. Shortcut: think of a secret that is no longer kept in the bag. Trap (A): Literal reading: the idiom is not about animals. Trap (B): Different meaning: it does not suggest a fight. Trap (D): Reversal: the idiom means the secret is revealed.

questions.concept_tag: One-word substitution - claustrophobia
questions.question_text: Choose the one word for 'an abnormal fear of closed spaces'.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The fear of closed or confined spaces is claustrophobia. Shortcut: 'claustro-' relates to closed or locked spaces. Trap (B): Opposite fear: agoraphobia is fear of open or crowded places. Trap (C): Different fear: acrophobia is fear of heights. Trap (D): Different fear: hydrophobia is fear of water.

questions.concept_tag: Prepositions - since and for
questions.question_text: Choose the correct option: She has been absent ___ Monday.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Since' is used with the present perfect and a starting point in time (Monday). Shortcut: 'since' + point in time; 'for' + length of time. Trap (A): Wrong: 'for' is followed by a length of time, such as 'for three days', not a point in time. Trap (C): Wrong: 'from' does not combine with the present perfect to indicate duration. Trap (D): Wrong: 'at' marks a point in time such as 'at noon' and is not used for a day here.

questions.concept_tag: Phrasal verbs - call off
questions.question_text: Choose the correct phrasal verb: The meeting was ___ because of heavy rain.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Call off' means to cancel an event. The meeting was cancelled because of the rain. Shortcut: the particle decides the meaning; learn them as units. Trap (A): Wrong: 'call on' means to visit or to request someone to speak. Trap (C): Wrong: 'call up' means to telephone or to summon for service. Trap (D): Wrong: 'call out' means to shout or to challenge.

questions.concept_tag: Subjunctive mood - were in an unreal condition
questions.question_text: Choose the correct option: If I ___ you, I would apologise.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In an unreal or hypothetical 'if' clause, the subjunctive 'were' is used for all persons. Shortcut: 'If I were you' is the fixed phrase for advice. Trap (A): Wrong in formal grammar: the subjunctive uses 'were' even for 'I'. Trap (B): Wrong: an unreal condition does not use the present indicative. Trap (C): Wrong: 'be' does not fit this construction.

questions.concept_tag: Parallel structure - gerunds in a list
questions.question_text: Choose the correct option: She likes singing, dancing and ___.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Items in a list should share the same grammatical form. 'Singing' and 'dancing' are gerunds, so the third item is 'painting'. Shortcut: match the form of the earlier items in the list. Trap (B): Wrong: it breaks the parallel pattern of -ing forms. Trap (C): Wrong: the base form does not match the other items. Trap (D): Wrong: the past form does not match the other items.

questions.concept_tag: Misplaced modifiers - participle phrase
questions.question_text: Choose the sentence in which the modifier is placed correctly.

options.A: Walking down the street, a dog barked at me.
options.B: A dog barked at me, walking down the street, I heard.
options.C: Walking down the street, the barking of a dog was heard.
options.D: Walking down the street, I heard a dog bark.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A participle phrase must describe the subject of the main clause. 'Walking down the street' describes 'I'. Shortcut: ask: who is doing the action in the opening phrase? Trap (A): Wrong: it suggests that the dog was walking down the street. Trap (B): Wrong: the word order is confused and the modifier is unattached. Trap (C): Wrong: the barking cannot be the one walking.

questions.concept_tag: Commonly confused words - affect and effect
questions.question_text: Choose the correct word: The committee's decision will ___ everyone in the school.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Affect' is the verb meaning to influence. After 'will', the base form 'affect' is used. Shortcut: 'A' for action (affect), 'E' for end result (effect). Trap (A): Wrong: 'effect' is generally a noun meaning result; as a verb it means to bring about. Trap (B): Wrong: 'will' needs the base form of the verb. Trap (D): Wrong: this is a noun form and cannot follow 'will'.

questions.concept_tag: Narration - question in indirect speech
questions.question_text: Choose the correct indirect speech: She asked me, "Where do you live?"

options.A: She asked me where do I live.
options.B: She asked me where I lived.
options.C: She asked me where I live?
options.D: She asked me that where I lived.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: In reported questions, the word order is subject + verb, there is no auxiliary 'do', and the tense shifts back: 'where I lived'. Shortcut: reported question = question word + statement order. Trap (A): Wrong: indirect questions use statement word order without 'do'. Trap (C): Wrong: the tense is not backshifted and the question mark is not required. Trap (D): Wrong: 'that' is not used before a question word.

questions.concept_tag: Voice - present continuous passive
questions.question_text: Choose the correct passive form of: 'They are building a bridge.'

options.A: A bridge is being built by them.
options.B: A bridge is built by them.
options.C: A bridge was being built by them.
options.D: A bridge has been built by them.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The present continuous passive is formed as 'is/are being + past participle'. Shortcut: keep the tense, change the form of 'be'. Trap (B): Wrong: this changes the continuous tense into the simple present. Trap (C): Wrong: this changes the present into the past. Trap (D): Wrong: this changes the tense to the present perfect.

questions.concept_tag: Punctuation - apostrophes in contractions
questions.question_text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.

options.A: Its a lovely day, isn't it?
options.B: It's a lovely day isn't it?
options.C: It's a lovely day, isn't it?
options.D: Its' a lovely day, isn't it?

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'It's' stands for 'it is'. A question tag is separated by a comma. Shortcut: expand the contraction to check: 'It is a lovely day'. Trap (A): Wrong: 'its' is a possessive; the contraction of 'it is' needs an apostrophe. Trap (B): Wrong: the tag question should be separated by a comma. Trap (D): Wrong: 'its'' does not exist in standard English.

questions.concept_tag: Prepositions and gerunds - despite
questions.question_text: Choose the correct option: Despite ___ hard, he failed the test.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Despite' is a preposition. It is followed by a noun or a gerund: 'despite working hard'. Shortcut: preposition + -ing form. Trap (A): Wrong: 'despite' takes a noun or a gerund, not a full clause. Trap (C): Wrong: 'despite' cannot be followed by an infinitive. Trap (D): Wrong: 'despite' needs a gerund, not a past form.

questions.concept_tag: Antonyms - benevolent
questions.question_text: Choose the word opposite in meaning to BENEVOLENT.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Benevolent means wishing to do good; 'malevolent' means wishing harm. The prefixes 'bene' and 'male' are opposites. Shortcut: bene- means good, male- means bad. Trap (A): Similar meaning: generous also shows kindness. Trap (B): Related but different: indifferent means not caring, which is not the direct opposite. Trap (C): Similar meaning: benign means gentle and harmless.

questions.concept_tag: Synonyms - lucid
questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to LUCID.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Lucid means easy to understand or clearly expressed, which is 'clear'. Shortcut: lucid comes from the Latin for light. Trap (B): Opposite meaning: confusing means hard to understand. Trap (C): Sound-alike word: lucky means fortunate. Trap (D): Sound-alike word: lazy means unwilling to work.

questions.concept_tag: Subject-verb agreement - each
questions.question_text: Choose the correct option: Each of the students ___ given a certificate.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Each' is a singular pronoun. The verb 'was' agrees with it, not with 'students'. Shortcut: each, either, neither, everyone take singular verbs. Trap (A): Wrong: 'each' is singular, so it needs a singular verb. Trap (B): Wrong: a plural helping verb does not agree with 'each'. Trap (D): Wrong: a plural verb does not agree with 'each', and the tense does not match.

questions.concept_tag: Tenses - future perfect
questions.question_text: Choose the correct option: By next year, she ___ her degree.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'By next year' signals an action completed before a future time, which needs the future perfect: 'will have completed'. Shortcut: 'by + future time' points to the future perfect. Trap (A): Wrong: it does not show that the action will be finished before a point in the future. Trap (C): Wrong: the present perfect does not match the future time 'next year'. Trap (D): Wrong: the simple present does not show completion before a future time.

questions.concept_tag: Para jumble - narrative sequence
questions.question_text:
Arrange the sentences in the correct order.
P: He therefore decided to return the money.
Q: Raju found a wallet on the road.
R: It contained a large sum and an identity card.
S: He traced the owner through the card.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Q introduces the wallet; R uses 'It' for the wallet and gives its contents; P gives the decision that follows ('therefore'); S describes how he acted on it. Order: QRPS. Shortcut: find the opener without pronouns or linkers, then follow the links. Trap (A): Wrong: P says 'therefore', which depends on the discovery of the contents in R, so P cannot come before R. Trap (B): Wrong: R says 'It', which needs a noun before it; the wallet is introduced in Q. Trap (C): Wrong: P begins with 'therefore' and cannot open the paragraph.

questions.concept_tag: Inversion - hardly and when
questions.question_text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.

options.A: Hardly he had reached the station when the train left.
options.B: Hardly had he reached the station than the train left.
options.C: Hardly he reached the station then the train left.
options.D: Hardly had he reached the station when the train left.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Rule: 'Hardly had + subject + past participle ... when ...' is used for one action immediately followed by another. Shortcut: 'hardly ... when', 'no sooner ... than'. Trap (A): Wrong: after 'hardly' at the start, the helping verb comes before the subject. Trap (B): Wrong: 'hardly' pairs with 'when', not 'than'. Trap (C): Wrong: the inversion is missing and 'then' is not the correct partner word.

questions.concept_tag: Synonyms - obsequious
questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to OBSEQUIOUS.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Obsequious means excessively eager to please or obey; 'fawning' has the same sense. Shortcut: obsequious = a servile flatterer. Trap (A): Sound-alike word: obstinate means stubborn. Trap (C): Sound-alike word: oblivious means unaware. Trap (D): Unrelated: generous means giving freely.

questions.concept_tag: Antonyms - loquacious
questions.question_text: Choose the word opposite in meaning to LOQUACIOUS.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Loquacious means very talkative; 'taciturn' means habitually silent. Shortcut: loqu- refers to speech; look for the quiet word. Trap (B): Same meaning: garrulous also means talkative. Trap (C): Different meaning: eloquent means expressive in speech. Trap (D): Different meaning: audacious means bold.

questions.concept_tag: Idioms - Gordian knot
questions.question_text: Choose the correct meaning of the phrase 'to cut the Gordian knot'.

options.C: to give up a hard task
options.D: to solve a difficult problem by a bold stroke

questions.pedagogical_explanation: According to the legend, Alexander cut through an impossibly tangled knot with his sword. The idiom means solving a tough problem decisively. Shortcut: recall the legend behind the idiom. Trap (A): Literal reading: the phrase does not refer to making knots. Trap (B): Different meaning: the idiom is not about relationships. Trap (C): Reversal: the idiom means solving the problem, not abandoning it.

questions.concept_tag: One-word substitution - plutocracy
questions.question_text: Choose the one word for 'government by the rich'.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Greek 'ploutos' means wealth, so government by the wealthy is plutocracy. Shortcut: use the root: pluto- means wealth. Trap (B): Different term: aristocracy means rule by the nobility. Trap (C): Different term: autocracy means rule by one person. Trap (D): Different term: theocracy means rule by religious leaders.

questions.concept_tag: Subject-verb agreement - the number of
questions.question_text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.

options.A: The number of applicants have increased this year.
options.B: A number of applicants has increased this year.
options.C: The number of applicants has increased this year.
options.D: The numbers of applicant has increased this year.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'The number of' takes a singular verb, because the subject is 'number'. 'A number of' means 'many' and takes a plural verb. Shortcut: the number = singular; a number of = plural. Trap (A): Wrong: 'the number' is singular, so the verb should be 'has'. Trap (B): Wrong: 'a number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb; also the meaning does not fit. Trap (D): Wrong: the noun forms do not agree.

questions.concept_tag: Prepositions - insist on
questions.question_text: Choose the correct preposition: He insisted ___ paying the bill.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Insist' takes 'on'. After a preposition, use a gerund: 'insisted on paying'. Shortcut: learn verb-preposition pairs. Trap (B): Wrong: 'insist at' is not used. Trap (C): Wrong: 'insist for' is not used. Trap (D): Wrong: 'insist to' is not used with a gerund.

questions.concept_tag: Subjunctive mood - suggest that
questions.question_text: Choose the correct option: I suggest that he ___ the report today.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: After verbs such as suggest, insist, demand and recommend, a 'that' clause takes the base form (the mandative subjunctive): 'he submit'. Shortcut: suggest/insist/demand + that + base form. Trap (B): Wrong: after 'suggest that', the subjunctive base form is used, not the -s form. Trap (C): Wrong: the past form does not fit the subjunctive. Trap (D): Wrong: the subjunctive does not take 'will'.

questions.concept_tag: Word usage - principal and principle
questions.question_text: Choose the sentence in which the word principal or principle is used correctly.

options.A: He is a man of strong principal.
options.B: The principal reason for the delay was heavy rain.
options.C: The school principle addressed the students.
options.D: She stuck to her principals despite pressure.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Principal' as an adjective means main; as a noun, it means the head of a school. 'Principle' means a rule or belief. Shortcut: principal = main or pal-person; principle = rule. Trap (A): Wrong: 'principle' (a rule or belief) is needed. Trap (C): Wrong: 'principal' (the head of a school) is needed. Trap (D): Wrong: 'principles' (beliefs) is needed.

questions.concept_tag: Analogies - quarantine and embargo
questions.question_text: Choose the pair that completes the analogy. Quarantine : Disease :: Embargo : ?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A quarantine restricts movement to stop a disease from spreading; an embargo restricts trade with a country. Shortcut: find what is being restricted in the first pair. Trap (A): Wrong: an embargo is a restriction, not a conflict. Trap (C): Wrong: an embargo is not about peace. Trap (D): Wrong: an embargo bans trade, whereas a tax charges for it.

questions.concept_tag: Vocabulary in context - inflammatory
questions.question_text: Choose the correct word: The minister's ___ remarks angered the opposition.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Inflammatory' describes words that arouse anger or hostility. Shortcut: inflame the crowd, so inflammatory words. Trap (A): Wrong: 'inflammable' means easily set on fire, and is used for physical objects. Trap (B): Wrong: 'infamous' means notorious for something bad. Trap (C): Wrong: 'infirm' means weak or frail.

questions.concept_tag: Sentence completion - contrast
questions.question_text: Choose the best word: Although the plan seemed ___, it proved remarkably effective.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Although' signals contrast: the plan seemed poor, yet proved effective. 'Unpromising' fits. Shortcut: 'although' reverses the direction of the sentence. Trap (A): Wrong: 'although' needs a negative first part, but foolproof is positive. Trap (B): Wrong: popularity does not contrast with being effective. Trap (D): Wrong: cost does not contrast with effectiveness.

questions.concept_tag: Voice - interrogative to passive
questions.question_text: Choose the correct passive form of: 'Who wrote this letter?'

options.B: By whom this letter was written?
options.C: By whom was this letter written?
options.D: Who is this letter written by?

questions.pedagogical_explanation: In the passive form of a 'who' question, 'who' becomes 'by whom', and the helping verb 'was' comes before the subject. Shortcut: who becomes by whom. Trap (A): Wrong: the agent needs the preposition 'by'. Trap (B): Wrong: the helping verb must come before the subject in a question. Trap (D): Wrong: it changes the tense to the present.

questions.concept_tag: Narration - request in indirect speech
questions.question_text: Choose the correct indirect speech: He said to me, "Please help me."

options.A: He said to me please help me.
options.B: He requested me that I help him.
options.C: He told me that I must help him.
options.D: He requested me to help him.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A request in direct speech is reported with 'requested' + object + infinitive. The pronoun 'me' becomes 'him'. Shortcut: please = requested. Trap (A): Wrong: the request is not converted. Trap (B): Wrong: the construction is not used for requests in this form. Trap (C): Wrong: this changes the request into an order.

questions.concept_tag: Correlatives - not only but also
questions.question_text: Choose the correct word to fill in the blank: Not only did she win the prize ___ she also broke the record.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Not only ... but also' is a correlative pair. The word 'but' completes the pair. Shortcut: 'not only' calls for 'but (also)'. Trap (A): Wrong: the pair 'not only' needs 'but (also)'. Trap (C): Wrong: it suggests result, but the sentence adds information. Trap (D): Wrong: it shows contrast, but the sentence adds information.

questions.concept_tag: Collective nouns - committee
questions.question_text: Choose the sentence that is correct.

options.A: The committee have submitted its report.
options.B: The committees has submitted its report.
options.C: The committee has submitted its report.
options.D: The committee has submit its report.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A committee acting as a unit takes a singular verb and the pronoun 'its'. 'Has' needs a past participle. Shortcut: keep verb and pronoun consistent. Trap (A): Wrong: the verb is plural but the pronoun 'its' is singular. Trap (B): Wrong: 'committees' is plural and does not agree with 'has'. Trap (D): Wrong: after 'has', use the past participle 'submitted'.

questions.concept_tag: Spelling - accommodation
questions.question_text: Choose the correctly spelt word.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The correct spelling has double c and double m: 'accommodation'. Shortcut: two c's and two m's. Trap (A): Wrong: it needs a double c. Trap (C): Wrong: it needs a double m. Trap (D): Wrong: it needs a double c and a double m.

questions.concept_tag: Idioms - add fuel to the fire
questions.question_text: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'to add fuel to the fire'.

options.C: to make a bad situation worse

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The idiom means doing something that increases anger or trouble that already exists. Shortcut: fuel makes fire stronger; the problem grows. Trap (A): Literal reading: the idiom is not about cooking. Trap (B): Reversal: the idiom means making matters worse. Trap (D): Unrelated: the idiom has nothing to do with saving.

questions.concept_tag: Words often confused - imply and infer
questions.question_text: Choose the correct word: The speaker's silence ___ that he disagreed.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: To 'imply' is to suggest without stating. The silence suggested his disagreement. Shortcut: speaker implies, listener infers. Trap (B): Wrong: a speaker implies; the listener infers. Trap (C): Wrong: 'implicate' means to involve someone in a wrong. Trap (D): Wrong: it does not fit the sense of suggesting something.
